body:
> I know the spec says that the OS compositor /should/ correctly convert between formats, but I have absolutely no faith that every single OS compositor will. I'm not confident /any/ of them will get it right the first time

On HDR displays, Windows 11 still gets sRGB wrong, and many HDR displays are terrible themselves, so I understand your hesitation, but things work differently on Wayland. Colorspaces are very strictly defined, and conversions between them are simple mathematical formulae that so far not a single compositor has gotten wrong.

Preventing conversions is a good thing in general, targeting the compositor's preferred colorspace is absolutely the right move for performance reasons, but assuming that the entire rest of the stack is completely broken and that you need to *attempt* to work around it before even seeing a single actual issue is a terrible approach.

You won't even always have a choice - in many cases, KDE Plasma will tell you to target a colorspace that uses the native primaries and whitepoint of the display + a gamma 2.2 transfer function with HDR headroom, rather than some standard HDR colorspace. Sometimes this is for compositor-side optimizations, but sometimes it's also just how the display works: The Steam Deck OLED for example uses a conventional gamma 2.2 transfer function.

Unless you add support for that, using Wayland instead of Vulkan to tell the compositor that you're targeting this special color space (which would be cool tbf, and could prevent color conversions on SDR displays as well), you're just gonna have to trust the compositor to convert whatever colorspace you use to what it actually needs.

> hdr on sdr monitors working on kwin is not enough, can we be confident all compositors will have a sufficiently robust implementation?

I think the above answers that question, but to expand on that, I would recommend you to detect if you should prefer HDR by checking `max_luminance > reference_luminance`.  If the compositor can make HDR work nicely on a given screen, no matter how that works under the hood, it'll just tell you by sending matching luminance values in the preferred image description.

Allowing the user or developer to manually enable HDR even when that's not the case might be nice to test the compositor's tone mapping capabilities, but isn't something you really need to care about.

> Yes we should prefer dynamic metadata to static metadata when setting hdr luminances. Dynamic metadata being system/screen luminance and hdr api. Static metadata being the project settings and bt.2408 recommendations.

That's not right. Static metadata - or more specifically the part of it that's called the mastering display information - describes the display the content was made for.

On Wayland, the preferred image description tells you about the display to target, so assuming you tonemap for that, you should also use those same values as the static HDR metadata, which tells the compositor that you're targeting the display you're supposed to, and that it shouldn't do any tone mapping.

If you don't target the system provided values, then the luminance ranges the developer manually set up should be used - representing the display they optimized the game for - and the compositor will tonemap it to the display it actually gets presented on.

Dynamic metadata would give the compositor more information about the actually used brightness ranges in a given scene, which may be lower than what the target display is capable of. As this is for better tonemapping, which you want to avoid in most cases anyways, and Wayland doesn't even have an extension for dynamic HDR metadata yet, you really don't have to worry about it right now.

> The "HDR" representation that engines use internally is actually higher range than current HDR display standards!

I think it's more helpful there to talk about the meaning of the brightness values rather than just their range. The internal data is normally scene-referred, it represents the brightness that things would have in the real world (assuming a "realistic" scene), and the output data takes into account the light adaptation of the viewer, and as you said of course the capabilities of the display.

body:
> Applied some of the tonemapping changes that @allenwp was playing around with since they seem to improve the result significantly.
> 
> Also gave me a chance to refactor the tonemap shader to remove parameters I was no longer using.

Thanks! I wanted to adapt your glow changes to this approach to review how it would behave with the different glow modes and a "Linear" tonemapper. Sometimes glow is used to simulate a physical effect (fog glow around a bright point of light), other times it is used as a psychological/perception trick to make part of an image appear brighter than the display can reproduce, or it can even be used as a stylistic effect with no physical or psychological basis.

I will reiterate that the intent behind this approach is to demonstrate that it is not possible to adapt any of the existing filmic tonemapper equations to HDR, as the contrast curve is not correctly scaled. Because Reinhard does not have a "toe", it is reasonable to adapt it to HDR using this approach, but it breaks when `white < (max_luminance / ref_luminance)`, so it likely makes the most sense to simply create a new HDR Reinhard tonemapper that has a `white = max(white, (max_luminance / ref_luminance);` statement, alongside the new filmic HDR tonemappers when they are introduced.

(A good example of when this breaks is setting Reinhard `white` to `1.0`, which by definition should be identical to Linear. Another example would be setting `white` to `2.0`, which is a reasonable value if you are targeting the Mobile rendering method: you will notice that the contrast and brightness between HDR and SDR is very different on all of the tonemappers. With higher `white` values, the difference in contrast is more subtle, but still incorrect in HDR mode.)

body:
Regarding ACES 2 support: I had a discussion with one of the members of ACES about how things should be handled with an operating system that scales its SDR content when displaying it in an HDR signal, instead of pinning SDR content at exactly 100 nits.

https://community.acescentral.com/t/aces-2-in-game-engines-variable-reference-max-luminance/5734

The summary is: there is no recommendation on how to deal with this and it would need to be researched. Regardless, I think I came up with a way to [best handle this](https://community.acescentral.com/t/aces-2-in-game-engines-variable-reference-max-luminance/5734/6?u=allenwp) by using `max_luminance` and `reference_luminance` values, but it is yet to be tested. I first need to write an ACES 2 reference implementation in glsl that could accept these parameters and then figure out how to simplify and approximate it.

I could say that a truly correct ACES 2 implementation would force `reference_luminance` to `100`, but I believe this has a notable downside of creating an game that has a very different brightness between SDR and HDR output.

I could go even further to say that Godot should always force `reference_luminance` to `100`, full stop, and this would allow ACES 2 to be absolutely correct in HDR and more obviously incorrect in SDR (because SDR would appear brighter on most systems). I don't think I agree with this; it's better to just let the developer/player set their `reference_luminance` to `100` if they want ACES HDR to be absolutely "correct". We simply don't have the ability to make ACES SDR game output correct on Windows when in Windows is in HDR output mode.

body:
I had a conversation with David Sena, an experienced rendering engineer, at GDC and he presented a really great idea with how to improve the workflow for a game that supports SDR and HDR output: **previewing HDR and SDR at the same time when lighting a scene and configuring exposure/tonemapping**. (Thanks, David!)

I thought about how this sort of feature might work in Godot and realized that the two viewports for HDR and SDR already exist in Godot: simply use the "Camera Preview" feature in the editor and run the scene (F6). The only remaining feature is a way to make the HDR setting different between the scene that is running in its own process and the editor. My proposal is to add a new HDR button to the Game workspace:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/71716f41-89a4-426a-97c7-d396c74e22ed)

This HDR button would ideally match the state of the scene instance that is running and, importantly, will not affect the project setting that used by the editor. This way, you can very quickly and easily light a scene and adjust your environment settings while previewing the look in SDR and HDR.

(Edit: I should also add that this feature can be implemented in a separate PR if desired, although I think this would be really great to have in the first Godot release that supports HDR output.)

Edit 2: This goes way outside of the scope of this PR and should exist in a separate proposal, but I'm mentioning it here because it doesn't make sense to make a proposal until HDR output is merged... Some people might be interested in being able to preview what a sRGB 2.2 power reference display looks like with the SDR version of the game when Windows HDR is enabled. This can be done by applying this to the final render of the game:
``` glsl
// Simulate sRGB display
color = linear_to_srgb(color); // sRGB encoding
color = pow(color, vec3(2.2)); // linearize like a reference sRGB display would
```
([This video](https://youtu.be/NzhUzeNUBuM) has more information about why linearization performed by a some sRGB displays does not match the inverse of sRGB nonlinear encoding used by Windows HDR.)

Edit 3: I did [some more research](https://allenwp.com/blog/2025/05/06/why-windows-srgb-sdr-over-hdr-is-technically-correct/) on the matter, and I believe it would be best to **not** include the "sRGB 2.2 power function reference display" preview that I suggested in my second edit. Instead, it's probably best to simply "follow the host operating system's behaviour for SDR content" for now. If there's strong demand for this sort of emulation, we can revisit it, but if we go that route, we'd probably want simulation of 2.2 sRGB displays as well as 2.4 BT.1886 TVs...

System info: Windows 11, NVIDIA GPU + AMD integrated graphics.

**Issue 1: Crash when running editor or game on secondary display.**

**Edit:** More details on this crash [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3009080786) and a [fix to the the issue here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3062944561).

**Issue 2: HDR output nonfunctional on AMD output**

When my AMD integrated graphics output is the primary display, HDR output does not function. This is the case regardless of whether I have a secondary display using my NVIDIA output. Interestingly, if I toggle HDR output on while the window is on my secondary NIVIDA output, I can move the window back to my AMD output and HDR output works on the AMD output until I toggle HDR output off and on again.

**June 26 edit:** This issue is a big and complex one, so I've make a [dedicated comment to describe it in more detail](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3010300661).

**Issue 3: `get_window().hdr_output_reference_luminance` does not update immediately**

I've noticed that when I change the Windows "SDR content brightness" slider and have "use screen luminance" enabled, Godot only responds to the change in reference luminance after I move or resize the Godot window. Maybe this is a reasonable behaviour, but I figured I'd mention it anyway. **Edit:** Actually, it seems that Mac maps its system brightness setting [to this sort of screen reference luminance in its "EDR" paradigm](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/metal/performing-your-own-tone-mapping#Map-Your-Content-to-the-Available-Range), so Godot will need to adjust its reference luminance in realtime to support this behaviour on Mac OS with `didChangeScreenParametersNotification`. Maybe there's a notification like this for Windows as well?

body:
I spent some time prototyping [different approaches to an HDR settings menu](https://github.com/allenwp/hdr-settings-menu) that might exist in a Godot game using this PR.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e1dabba9-aa5f-4d4b-80cf-a57b8f0855ae

I found that it was easy to implement most of the menu styles, except that a number of the styles require one modification to this PR: separate `use_screen_max_luminace` and `use_screen_reference_luminance` settings.

Note: I used the term "**Brightness**" instead of "reference luminance" because this is the correct player-facing term. In my opinion, it does not make sense for a game to present the term "reference luminance" to the player when all it really means is just the overall brightness of the game when using HDR output. I am indifferent on which term is used by Godot scripting/project settings.

**Style A - Simple**
Separate brightness and max luminance controls that default to screen values.

**Style B - Advanced**
Same as "Style A - Simple", but with nits values always presented to the player, even when they have not been customized.

**Style C - Ignore Screen Lum.**
Screen luminance is entirely ignored. For games designed to be played in a home cinema or where the viewing environment's brightness is known in advance.

**Style D - Screen Luminance Toggle**
One toggle switch that controls whether screen luminance is used or custom luminance is used for both brightness and max luminance.

**Style E - Screen Luminance (Saved)**
Same as "Style D - Screen Luminance Toggle", except the player's previous brightness and max luminance values are restored when they turn off "Use screen luminance".

**Style F - Automatic Simple**
"Use screen luminance" is automatically disabled when the user changes either brightness or max luminance. "Use screen luminance" is automatically enabled when the user presses the "Reset" button. My personal favourite style.

**Another Style Idea (not in video)**
Because the reference luminance value is simply the SDR white level Windows setting, the Brightness control could be omitted entirely and reference luminance would always match screen reference luminance. Only max luminance would be configurable through the game.

I have a pretty strong preference towards **Style F - Automatic Simple** because it makes for a very simple GUI that integrates naturally with other game settings that I could imagine. For this GUI to function correctly, it needs separate `use_screen_max_luminace` and `use_screen_reference_luminance` settings.

body:
I [mentioned before](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-2755675325) that it would be great if users could preview SDR alongside of HDR while configuring their game's lighting and environment settings. I have another idea that I think might be useful and worth exploring. Maybe this makes sense for this PR or maybe it should be in a separate, future PR.

When working with HDR displays, it is common for them to tonemap internally, especially if you are not using an expensive reference display that allows for turning off this sort of internal tonemapping. In practice, this makes it very hard to use a low-to-mid range consumer HDR display to author HDR content. This can be made even worse by auto-dimming and other features that change the image in HDR mode.

So what I've been doing with my work is simulating HDR with my SDR display. This is pretty trivial:

```
max_val = max_luminance / ref_luminance;
output /= max_val;
```

If I crank up my SDR display to max brightness and turn the lights off in my room, it lets me see what the highlights of my HDR image might be without any HDR display tonemapping obfuscating the image. For this to really work 100% correctly, you would need an sRGB display that decodes the SDR signal with a piecewise function to match HDR behaviour, but even using a reference sRGB display with a 2.2 power function decoding will work quite well for viewing the highlights specifically.

I'm really not sure how this tooling could exist in Godot or if it could be implemented in a plugin in the future. Regardless, I expect that many users who are looking to implement HDR support will have a lot of struggles when using their normal consumer HDR display to author their game, just as I have when working on tonemapping for HDR...

author: allenwp

body:
If it still matters, it is impossible for Wayland to implement the `screen_*` methods in the way that is expected.
We are able to implement all methods by using the real screen data but we are unable to know which screen a window is on.

The problem with that is using `screen_is_hdr_supported` as a condition for enabling hdr on a window would quickly become flaky if the window is not in the first screen (as would all other things that are based on screen). The workaround I have implemented is to ignore the screen data and instead use the main window's hdr information (which on wayland is extensive enough for this to work). 

This should hopefully work unless sub-windows are placed on different screens to the main window with different hdr capabilities which is hopefully enough of an edge case for it to not matter.

If the workaround seems sufficient then that's good and we're done. If it isn't then the only way I could think of that this API could be more robust under wayland is to either move or duplicate the `screen_*` methods to `window_*` methods. Ie either replace `screen_is_hdr_supported` with `window_is_hdr_supported` or have `window_is_hdr_supported` in addition to `screen_is_hdr_supported`.
author: ArchercatNEO

body:
Yeah, all screen-based APIs are quite painful to implement in Wayland, if not impossible. You can know which screens the window is on but not which you're mostly into, with the idea that the compositor should tell you the best settings.

Because of this, I support with moving to window-based APIs wherever possible (`window_*` instead of `screen_`)

body:
For Apple / #106814, the HDR demo project works 🥳

When the main window is HDR enabled, popup windows are rendered incorrectly, as they are SDR.

The issue is the changes to the `RenderCompositorRD` (`_ensure_blit_pipelines` specifically) assume the blit pipelines are the same for all windows by using the `MAIN_WINDOW_ID` as the reference. This is not the case (at least on macOS) if the main window is HDR (RGBA 16-bit float) and the popup window is SDR (RGBA8 UNORM). I would imagine the issue is the same on Windows?

This issue is confirmed for both the Metal and Vulkan (MoltenVK) renderers

> @DarkKilauea Please let me know if you'd like me to review the comments in this PR and make a checklist in your initial comment with the outstanding items. I should have time for this sometime in the next week or two...

I've been trying to keep track of the pending items as we go, even as I haven't had the time to do anything about them.  Here is my current TODO list:

- Turning on HDR output should implicitly turn on hdr_2d on the main viewport.
    - Doing so in the project settings should automatically update all viewports in the editor that need it as well.
- Compare performance of 10-bit and 16-bit swap buffers and choose an appropriate default.
    - I'm tempted to make `16-bit` color the default, but I don't want to hurt performance unnecessarily here.
- Fix user set luminance values getting overwritten by `use_screen_luminance`.
    - Yes, the documentation is wrong about the luminance settings being fallbacks for `use_screen_luminance`. That was true at one point, isn't anymore after some refactoring.
- Replace `use_screen_luminance` with `auto_adjust_max_luminance` and `auto_adjust_reference_luminance`
    - Idea stems from Allen's comment up above that there may be value in overriding these individually. There is also confusion created by the term `use_screen_luminance` that may relieved if the property doesn't indicate how Godot auto adjusts the values. I'm hoping this will clear the way for the Wayland implementation to implement the auto adjust as is best for that framework.
- Fix blit pipelines not being created for each swap chain.
    - Bug reported by @stuartcarnie, thanks!
- Document that support for `screen_` methods is optional and may not be available on all platforms.
    - I think both Wayland and macOS may need some wiggle room to not implement the `screen_` methods, these should be informational, not required.
- Fix negative color values sneaking into the blit pass leading to off colors.
    - Reported by @allenwp, may need to double check this as the scRGB space allows negative colors and we don't want to lose color detail in the rec 709 linear space Godot is effectively using internally.
- Incorporate tonemapping changes from @allenwp into this PR.
    - I want to be judicious here and avoid blowing up the size of this PR. Some changes, such as those to AgX should probably be in their own PR since support for `white` isn't in mainline Godot yet afaik.
- Update PR description to explain that it implements an EDR (extended display range) approach instead of tonemapping content up to the range of the display.
    - I think the PR description needs another pass on it to clarify some details and make it more presentable as a major feature in a version of Godot.
- Investigate crash bugs on AMD/NVidia GPU combined systems.
    - I'll need some help here as I don't have a system with this configuration. I suspect we might be running into some driver issues here, but it is hard to be sure.

As for when this can be merged, I'm not sure. Godot tends to require a general consensus in order to merge, which can take a long time to get, but generally leads to better thought out contributions. I could use some help in prioritizing the outstanding work and making a cut line for what is needed to get this into Godot and start testing with the general user base. body:
Update:

Added support for automatically setting `hdr_2d` on viewports when the window enables HDR output. This should remove the need to set `rendering/viewport/hdr_2d` in project settings in order to get the increased dynamic range expected.

However, if you are creating custom viewports, you may need to set `hdr_2d` on that viewport in addition to `tonemap_to_window` if you intend that viewport to be show on screen with HDR output enabled. There is a new warning that will try to catch the most likely scenarios where this may occur.

However after working through the possible scenarios, I am forced to conclude that it is impossible to catch them all. A example of such a case is a viewport that renders to a texture with `hdr_2d` off, but then tries to render that texture with the full dynamic range in an HDR output enabled window. With no link between the viewport that rendered the texture and the window itself, there is no way to detect the mismatch in settings. I don't think such cases are a blocker, just something to be aware of.

body:
> @allenwp Please let me know if the `window_set_hdr_output_auto_adjust_reference_luminance` and `window_set_hdr_output_auto_adjust_max_luminance` methods (or their versions on `Window`) doesn't provide what you need to implement your recommended approach for a HDR setting screen.

Separating the two settings works great! I'm now able to implement every style of settings menu that I can think of. Thanks!

@stuartcarnie did a bit of work on EDR support on Apple platforms and we chatted a bit about it in RocketChat... I think on iOS it makes sense to **not** allow either `hdr_output_auto_adjust_reference_luminance` or `hdr_output_auto_adjust_max_luminance` to be set to `false` because the display information about max luminance should be accurate and the reference luminance is controlled through the device brightness setting. Alternatively, we could "simulate"/force user control of max and reference luminance by adjusting what we're writting to the buffer based on the device configuration, but I'm not sure how often users will want to have this sort of control, as its against the design paridigm of the iOS platform (it would effectively be overriding the device brightness setting, which is often a bad idea because it makes the user think their phone's brightness controls are broken).

I'm not sure about MacOS, because you may have an HDR TV connected to your Mac which would need the same sort of user control that a Windows PC would need when connected to that TV.

Anyway, the reason I bring it up is because if we go the route of preventing the auto-adjust properties from being set to `false` on iOS (and possibly other platforms), another `hdr_output_can_disable_auto_adjust_luminance` property (or maybe a feature tag / constant) would be needed to allow the game developer to adjust their in-game settings menu based on the platform.

body:
@allenwp I took a look at clipping values in the blit shader to avoid negative values.

I'm not sure this is correct for the Rec. 2020 color space, negative values from the perspective of Rec. 709 should be expected if you are trying to encode values in Rec. 2020.

For example, if we look at the color space testers in the `hdr_output_tester` project and lay them on top of each other:
![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/47caae13-14c6-441e-b6e2-fb0f62cadeea)

Everything outside of the sRGB/Rec. 709 space has a negative component. Clipping those components to zero should lead to a loss of color detail anywhere outside of the Rec. 709 space.

I double checked both your version of the PR (thanks for the recent rebase!) and this PR with RenderDoc and noticed that the negative values are clipped in your version in the final output, even in linear mode.

In this PR, those values are passed through in linear mode, and in HDR 10 mode the colors are converted to values that no longer have negative components in Rec. 2020 space.

body:
> However if you move the slider around (implicitly disabling `auto_adjust`) and then change luminance in system settings the window luminance changes a bit but not to the actual compositor luminance since hitting reset changes it again.
> Is this expected behavior in HDR (is it the expected behaviour under windows?)

I believe what you've demonstrated here is the behaviour of the HDR to SDR tonemapper of KDE Plasma. In the case of simulating HDR on an SDR monitor, the "Maximum SDR Brightness" setting that you've adjusted acts as an input to the KDE Plasma tonemapping functions that do this mapping of HDR to SDR. So this means that changing this system setting will impact how HDR is mapped to SDR, and thus change the way the image appears. It's not easily visible with this test project, but I suspect the HDR to SDR tonemapping behaviour is changing when you change the "Maximum SDR Brightness" setting regardless of whether `hdr_output_auto_adjust_reference_luminance` is enabled or not.

So in the end, I think this is expected and I believe that you would not see this behaviour at all when using an HDR display with no system-level HDR/SDR conversion.

> One small suggestion I could make is perhaps make the `auto_adjust` flags more explicit? From basic testing it seems hitting reset enables it and moving the slider disables it but maybe it would be better if there was an explicit toggle which enabled/disabled the slider?

Thanks for the feedback! You're right in your understanding. I played around with this approach in [my prototype project](https://github.com/allenwp/hdr-settings-menu) and took a guess that the automatic switching I used in my latest test project would be the most reasonable for players who know nothing about HDR and want simple and optional HDR settings. Of course, this would be at most an example project and won't affect Godot's internals at all -- game developers can do whatever they'd like. But I'm curious to hear more feedback about this from others and some player testing would definitely be valuable... I should also mention that I modeled this "automatic" settings approach off of Ratchet and Clank's Maximum Luminance setting, which behaves exactly like this: pressing "reset" changes max luminance to be automatic and based on your display, while adjusting the slider disables this automatic behaviour and forces the user's custom maximum lumiance:

body:
> @allenwp I took a look at clipping values in the blit shader to avoid negative values.
>
> I'm not sure this is correct for the Rec. 2020 color space, negative values from the perspective of Rec. 709 should be expected if you are trying to encode values in Rec. 2020.

I believe I’m familiar with the colour science and colorimetry at play here. And from a pure colorimetric perspective, you’re entirely correct! Simple compositing and colour functions behave correctly regardless of positive or negative values and should be clipped to non-negative at the latest point possible, which would be to BT.2020 in HDR buffer writing (the blit file in Godot) and clipped again later to some other space based on the primaries of the display hardware. It is for this reason that Windows is able to correctly do compositing in ScRGB (aka “extended sRGB”) space, even though it has negative values.

So I asked Stephen Hill about his thoughts of using something like ScRGB as a working space in Godot and he was quick to caution against the idea because some lighting simulation formulas do not produce correct results with negative values. Of course, this does not mean that this applies to the current state of Godot’s lighting simulation, which may not include these formulas, but future versions of Godot might use these formulas. Additionally, Godot allows for negative lights, which are useful, but also non-physical, so it’s undefined what their “correct” behaviour should be. My opinion is that Godot should attempt to be “correct” with all positive values so long as the user is not actively introducing negative light into the scene with negative lights, which allows for best-case physically correct simulation, regardless of what lighting formulas are used now or in the future.

Further to this, many tonemapping functions do not behave correctly with negative input values, so maintaining consistency between Linear and other tonemappers allows for less unexpected scenarios. This clipping to sRGB already happens implicitly for the Linear tonemapper when writing to an SDR buffer, so it should also happen for HDR buffers.

So to support wide colour space, the correct approach is likely to allow the game developer to switch the internal working colour space to a wide gamut space like BT.2020 or ACEScg. This allows all simulation to be performed on positive RGB values, which will allow for the most correct results possible with any RGB based simulation formulas. Adding a new working space is outside of the scope of this PR and likely only makes sense to merge after HDR support has been merged. According to this logic, I believe that it is a bug that textures can currently be imported with negative values, but it doesn’t make sense to change this behaviour until support for other RGB working spaces has been added to Godot. Once a wide gamut working space is available as an option in Godot, we can “simply” clip all RGB values to the working colour space at import time, and additionally clip to the working space again just before blit to give consistent behaviour of negative lights between SDR and HDR modes when using the sRGB working space.

I wrote a lot there and made a few assumptions, so it’s possible that some things I wrote aren’t entirely correct. Regardless, I believe there is a lot of value to developing HDR support in a way that allows developers to take an existing SDR game, enable HDR output, and get a result that closely matches the visuals that they fine tuned based on negative value clipping in the sRGB SDR working space. Because most users of Godot are not experts in colour science and lighting simulation, this approach of clipping to sRGB will give consistent and expected results, regardless of the behaviour of negative lights and HDR textures on lighting simulation. A separate PR to add a wide gamut working colour space (likely BT.2020) is needed.

To put this in a more comical wording, my hope for HDR output support is to minimize the [WTF per minute](https://commadot.com/wtf-per-minute/) of game developers who take their existing SDR game and enable HDR output, regardless of what negative values they might have had accidentally bouncing around in their scene.

body:
> I think on iOS it makes sense to not allow either hdr_output_auto_adjust_reference_luminance or hdr_output_auto_adjust_max_luminance to be set to false because the display information about max luminance should be accurate and the reference luminance is controlled through the device brightness setting.

Definitely same on Wayland. The max luminance can change dynamically in some cases (like battery saving mode), and should always be configured system wide. Like on iOS, the reference luminance is (on some devices at least) controlled by the brightness setting.

> on an SDR monitor but HDR enabled in system settings anyway

Then it's not actually an SDR monitor. Or at least it claims to support HDR signalling :)

> I believe what you've demonstrated here is the behaviour of the HDR to SDR tonemapper of KDE Plasma. In the case of simulating HDR on an SDR monitor, the "Maximum SDR Brightness" setting that you've adjusted acts as an input to the KDE Plasma tonemapping functions that do this mapping of HDR to SDR. So this means that changing this system setting will impact how HDR is mapped to SDR, and thus change the way the image appears.

"Maximum SDR Brightness" is just a badly named setting (removed in that form in Plasma 6.4) that's for HDR displays only. Together with the normal brightness slider, it defines the reference luminance of the display.

If the reference luminance of the window doesn't match the display, the compositor will map it so that it does match (assuming Godot tells it about the reference that's actually used). Still, it does indeed also change the tone mapping curve. In the video the max luminance of content is 10000cd/m², but the display can only do 400, so KWin will do tone mapping, even with the display is in HDR mode.

> If you need a Linux user with a HDR display to test this, I have a Steam Deck OLED if this helps

Unfortunately SteamOS doesn't support the standard stuff yet. HDR output is possible in game mode only through Vulkan, and getting the display capabilities only works through Wine or gamescope-specific APIs. The desktop mode's Wayland session is also a bit too old with Plasma 6.2 (Plasma 6.3 added support for the non-experimental protocol).

body:
If the method turns out to be useful to scripting the best case for Wayland is if a window-based alternative is added.
If the method has no demand I would recommend removing the method until an actual use-case is found.

Wayland actually provides the same information for screens and windows, including things like max fall and max content light level. The issue is that all information on screens will be inaccurate due to the Wayland DisplayServer not knowing which screen a window is on (this is intended by the protocol which is why all information we could require of a window is associated with the window and not the screen it is on). So in terms of implementation as long as a `window` variant of `screen` methods exist we can implement it.

body:
> Is it possible to use `COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_LINEAR` with `DATA_FORMAT_A2R10G10B10_UNORM_PACK32` on all rendering drivers?

I think I can answer my own question: simply "no". 10 bits per channel isn't enough to store linear encoded values for the purpose of high quality HDR output.

So I think performance testing is still needed? My suspicion, backed by what was said in the NVIDIA presentation, is that supporting low precision mode will only reduce execution speed with minimal practical memory gain. In fact, I suspect that even just having the extra branching in the blit shader will present a measurable decrease in performance. (I have this suspicion because branching to different tonemappers in the tonemap shader decreases performance of the linear tonemapper.)

I'll try to get some performance testing done soon. It will be good to see at least FPS and memory usage stats for:
- High precision enabled, high precision disabled, and low precision removed entirely from the blit shader
- Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA
- Fullscreen and maximized window

I will also try to take a look into how well a low precision mode is supported on the other platforms. My suspicion is that, in spite of what Microsoft's documentation says, low precision mode is really only beneficial in terms of speed when you have 10-bit PQ encoded BT.2020 content, like a video file, that needs effectively no further transformations to put it into a `DATA_FORMAT_A2R10G10B10_UNORM_PACK32` container. Needing to convert to BT.2020 and do the 10-bit PQ encoding ourselves, combined with the additional blit branching, might be simply slower in practice on all platforms. Additionally, considering the 12-bit PQ encoded output signals of the future or a user configuring their PC with Dolby Vision output, a 10-bit PQ encoded buffer would definitely be slower because the host system would need to re-encode this to match the output signal.

Anyway, I'll stop my rambling now and try and get some real performance data :) All of this that I wrote is entirely conjecture right now!

body:
We've found that on the wayland pr we don't actually tell the compositor what our reference luminance is which leads our metadata being wrong and getting tonemapped incorrectly (this is likely the reason why my screenshots had such significant differences in brightness).

Effectively wayland requires that our hdr metadata is both correct and what the compositor wanted. If it is not the compositor will enforce its own metadata onto us to ensure good HDR. There is no option to disable this, we can only comply.

This would be fine except that the native vulkan driver will implicitly try to use the wayland protocol so that less capable apps can get tonemapped more accurately. Wayland requires that only one of the app and the vulkan driver provide metadata. To disable this behaviour we need to set our colorspace to `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT`. 

After that I believe there is already enough information to satisfy the wayland compositor. The hdr metadata we need to supply includes luminances (already handled), the primaries and the transfer function. I believe if the primaries and transfer function are "incorrect" the compositor can transform the data losslesly (ie loss of performance but not fidelity) so we do not require being able to set the colorspace, only being able to get it (which we can already do). If there is actual loss of fidelity from colorspace conversion then that would be a different significant issue to address but if there is only a loss of performance then it is acceptable for HDR V1.

If supporting `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` is too complex for HDR V1 it seems there is a workaround that could be kept wayland side but it seems like it only works because HDR10 having a default reference luminance of `203` allows for some special maths. https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102987#issuecomment-2997406654

I believe it would be best to not have workarounds but if `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` is too much work it can always be deferred to whatever PR adds support for additional colorspaces and would require changing the workaround.

body:
I will do my best to explain the mentality of the wayland devs when deciding upon this API.

There are apps which do not provide any metadata at all and are probably unaware of colorspaces outside sRGB. If metadata is missing **assume** the colorspaces is indeed sRGB and act accordingly (clip output into an sRGB range). This allows the majority of apps to look "mostly OK" on HDR displays.

There are apps which know what colorspace they render in but are unable to adapt to the native colorspace of the display. These apps should provide metadata so that the compositor can best transform the output to the display's native format. This is better than assuming clipping to sRGB if the app is rendering in anything other than sRGB.

There are apps which are both aware of their colorspace and can adapt to the display's native colorspace (like us). These apps will receive metadata from the compositor about what the best colorspace, luminances, etc it would be best for us to render with. If we are able to comply with these requirements then the compositor will have no further work to do and will (possibly) submit our output unmodified.

This is just listing the cases. Someone at some point needs to turn our rendered scene from the "realistic" luminance values with millions of nits into something the display can actually use. On windows this usually means apps bypassing the system and promising that their output is indeed correct. On wayland sending the correct format to the display is always enforced. If we do it ourselves there is no issue and the compositor leaves us alone, if we don't then the compositor has to step in and do it for us. Difference is if we don't behave and don't give the compositor hdr metadata then it will enforce that our output is sRGB and clip accordingly.

Both NVIDIA and AMD graphics drivers must be active in the Windows Device Manager. In this configuration, both outputs can be configured by Windows to have HDR output enabled.

## NVIDIA-connected display is primary display

In this scenario, both d3d12 and vulkan rendering drivers behave similarly: Whenever the Godot game window is on the AMD (secondary) display, the "screen supports HDR" and "window supports HDR" return false. Any time the window enters this display, HDR mode will be disabled. This basically behaves like this secondary screen is an SDR display, even though it has HDR enabled in the Windows display settings.

This scenario sounds like it's working "fine". But because my secondary AMD-connected display is set in Windows to be HDR enabled, I would expect that I should be able to use HDR in Godot, but I can't. That said, it all fails gracefully, so maybe there is nothing we can do about this (and it's a GPU driver behaviour we can't control???)

## AMD-connected display is primary display

In this scenario, I get different behaviour between the d3d12 driver and the vulkan driver:

### d3d12 driver
Both displays fully support HDR output in Godot. When a window is moved between displays and `hdr_output_enabled` is `true`, the game will remain having HDR output enabled without any issues.

### vulkan driver
Both displays have "screen supports HDR" and "window supports HDR" report `true`, so I expect `hdr_output_enabled` can be used, but...

**Window is on NVIDIA-connected (secondary) display**
HDR output works without issue.

**Window is on AMD-connected (primary) display**
HDR output gives the following warning and HDR output does not function, even though all HDR metadata (lumiance and HDR supported on the screen) is correctly retreived:

```
WARNING: HDR output requested but no HDR compatible format was found, falling back to SDR.
     at: RenderingDeviceDriverVulkan::_determine_swap_chain_format (drivers\vulkan\rendering_device_driver_vulkan.cpp:30
```

**Moving window from NVIDIA-connected (secondary) display to AMD-connected display**
In this scenario, if `hdr_output_enabled` was true when the window was on the NIVIDA-connected display, HDR output will continue to work perfectly fine on the AMD-connected display! ...until I toggle `hdr_output_enabled` or `prefer_high_precision` flags, at which point it will go back to behaving as it would have if the window was launched on this display (it will print the warning about no HDR compatible format being found).

**Moving window from AMD-connected (primary) display to NIVIDA-connected display**
In this scenario, `hdr_output_enabled` can be `true`, even though it is displaying as SDR. When the window is moved to the NVIDIA display, `hdr_output_enabled` will remain true, even though it is still SDR. Toggling `hdr_output_enabled` or `prefer_high_precision` will cause HDR output to start working again.

So this second set of issues that is specific to the AMD-connected display being the primary display are much more severe because the game thinks its rendering in HDR output when its not. I had an idea for getting hdr on vulkan working but my `vulkaninfo` reporting support for `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` while yours aren't is making me doubt it.

If for some reason the windows vulkan drivers don't check our colorspace is supported (and from what I've heard seemingly neither does windows) we could use `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` and just promise that the format we are using is supported by the display. This would avoid needing explicit support from the vulkan driver to use HDR output (which seemingly works just fine even without support) and would enable HDR on windows with vulkan on a wider range of hardware. It would also solve the Wayland issue I mentioned earlier which is convenient.

That of course depends on 2 things. First, we would need to know what formats the display actually supports with vulkan which as far as I'm aware still requires d3d12. However that's not really any worse than from the current state so we could put a pin in that for now. Secondly and more importantly, we would need the windows vulkan drivers to accept `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` without having given explicit support for it. I don't know that it would work but with how lenient HDR seems to be on Windows we could always just try to see if it works.

And if I were to push it, using `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` would require us to target the native colorspace of the display which unless my inexperience has me very mistaken is only one. If it really is only one then seemingly it might be easier to just declare to the vulkan driver what we want the colorspace to be from the DisplayServer instead of messing with `prefer_high_precision` and such (which conveniently also aligns with what is efficient for the wayland display server).

However if `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` isn't the trick to getting hdr working on incomplete drivers then it seems like it'd be best to have something like `is_hdr_output_supported`  on the rendering driver to check if it even supports an hdr colorspace to avoid bugs like Allen is encountering. (currently there are no checks that the vulkan driver actually supports any hdr colorspaces to report support for the screen or window supporting hdr. The only check is that the godot vulkan driver has hdr implemented (which is true) and the screen's colorspace is a particular hdr colorspace).

Finding information on `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` is quite hard so hopefully most of what I've said is correct. I do still believe the current vulkan on windows issues are due to native driver issues so unless we're coming up with workarounds like using `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` to bypass driver capabilities I don't believe there is much we can do.

body:
`VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` only has loosely defined semantics, but the best description for it is imo "pass through Vulkan" - it's meant for when you define the color space through other means than Vulkan, *not* for pass-through to the display or anything like that.

On Wayland, you want to use it when you define the color space through the color management protocol. If you don't set it through the protocol, then the result is implementation-defined (generally the compositor will assume sRGB though).

I don't know what the matching API would be on the Windows side, but if you don't use it, then you should not use `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT` either

body:
> With Reinhard tonemapping, this does a pretty good job at improving detail in bright areas compared to a SDR presentation through RTX HDR. (If I disable automatic reference luminance and set it to `200`, it will look as bright overall, except the highlights are no longer clipped.)

Hmm. I disagree that it is good behaviour for the upper clipping point to change when using the Reinhard tonemapper. This is why I [requested that `white_squared` should also be divided by `output_max_value`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#pullrequestreview-3002042639). The original spirit of the Reinhard tonemapper is that you set the upper clipping point (the `white` parameter) and it non-linearly compresses this input dynamic range into the output dynamic range.

The behaviour of this PR without this adjustment is that the `white` parameter is effectively being multiplied by `output_max_value`. While doing this maintains some of the nonlinear characteristic of the curve across different dynamic ranges, it makes it difficult for the author to say "everything below this linear scene value should not clip".

This was a hard decision for me to make, but the thing that convinced me this was a good idea was that if the user wants to have a `white` parameter that scales with `output_max_value`, then they can simply write a script that adjusts `white` dynamically by scaling it by `output_max_value`. This way with the default behaviour the user can have confidence that the `white` parameter is the actual upper clipping point, regardless of output dynamic range, and the Reinhard tonemapper will adjust its compression according to the output dynamic range.

Some videos showing how this works in practice are shown in the "high clip" and "Variable / Extended Dynamic Range" sections of [my blog post](https://allenwp.com/blog/2025/05/29/allenwp-tonemapping-curve/).

I believe the reason the current PR doesn't divide `white_squared` by `output_max_value` is simply because this operation was buried in a new function I added to `environment_storage.cpp` in my WIP prototype that the HDR version of Reinhard was taken from. This made it hard to discover this small detail.

(As an aside, I actually think the opposite should be done with AgX: I believe that it is better to favour maintaining the non-linearity of the curve for the AgX tonemapper because the specific non-linearity of the curve has a dramatic effect on hue shift with the AgX working colour space. I plan to add a note to the documentation that the `white` parameter for AgX is multiplied by the max output value, unlike other tonemappers. But this is very much an exception that needed to be done to make the AgX nonsense work nicely in practice.)

body: I have noticed that Windows returns the following for SDR displays: This highlights how Windows wasn't designed for the EDR paradigm: given these values, the max output value would be `3.375` for SDR instead of the expected `1.0`. From Godot's perspective, these are the correct and accurate luminance values that Windows is providing, so I guess it makes sense that we don't override them and simply state in the documentation that these luminance values might be nonsense if HDR is not supported on the screen. ...Or is this a "foot gun" and we should intentionally override these Windows-reported values with something that is more in-line with the EDR paradigm when the screen doesn't support HDR? If we override them, then I think the best defaults would be: - Min luminance: 0.0 - Max luminance: 200.0 - Max full frame luminance: 200.0 - SDR white level: 200.0 This would give a more EDR-compatable set of values when HDR is not supported by the screen. author: iuymatiao

body:
> @allenwp Is this occurring on a HDR400 monitor? If so, this might be a case where Windows is reporting the HDR luminance values of the monitor regardless of HDR actually being enabled. Are these luminance values supposed to be 0 or NaN when the screen is in SDR?

No, this is with SDR-only displays over either HDMI or DisplayPort, regardless of GPU. It seems to just be the default fallback that Windows provides. You can try this yourself with [my test project](https://github.com/allenwp/godot-hdr-output-test-project) and this PR, even if you don't have an HDR display, and I expect you'll see the same numbers.

> As for the SDR white level, I believe the industry has standardized around 100 nits, so my hunch is that we should probably be using this as well for the “mastering” SDR brightness. If users set their monitor brightness higher or lower than 100 nits, then there’s nothing we can really do about the SDR image deviating from “creative intent”.

My intent was to match the default project setting when "automatically adjust reference luminance" is disabled, which is 200.0 nits. Rationale for this is explained [in this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#pullrequestreview-2659049328).

Additionally, there are many industry standards:

- Reference luminance for sRGB is 80 nits.
- Reference luminance for authoring HDR for cinema (dark viewing environment) is 100 nits.
- Reference luminance for authoring HDR for use alongside SDR content (typical home/mobile viewing environment) is 203 nits.

Notably, when using tools like the Adobe Media Encoder, you can choose either 100 or 203 nits as a reference luminance for HDR video renders.

203 nits is most suitable for Godot, as games are often not played in a cinema-like (dark) environment, but 200.0 is a better user-facing value as described previously linked comment.

That said, we're talking about SDR on Windows, so using 80 nits for all three reference, max, and full frame max when in SDR mode could be a good option, as that matches the sRGB standard and also matches Windows default SDR White Level for SDR sRGB output.

body: > I have noticed that Windows returns the following for SDR displays: > > > ...Or is this a "foot gun" and we should intentionally override these Windows-reported values with something that is more in-line with the EDR paradigm when the screen doesn't support HDR? I think this is a foot gun. Windows is reporting here the capabilities of the display in terms of how bright it can be, but that doesn't mean it is an HDR display. When the display mode is SDR, the SDR white level doesn't seem to be used at all and values of `1.0` become the current brightness of the display, which can go up to the max brightness of that display. In Microsoft's documentation, this is described as the difference between display-referred brightness vs scene-referred brightness. SDR display modes seem to always be display-referred. This article is a decent place to start learning how Windows treats HDR content: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/direct3darticles/high-dynamic-range

> The Reinhard tonemapper isn't entirely complete in this version of the PR, but we can update it in a future PR before stable release. Specifically, when HDR output is enabled, the `white` parameter of this tonemapper must always be `>= output_max_value`, even when `output_max_value == 1.0`. To maintain historical SDR appearance, this should not be the case when HDR output is disabled. This behaviour is required for reasonable behaviour in the EDR paradigm when `white < output_max_value`.
> 
> The only "tricky" part is that there is currently no way to know if HDR is enabled within `environemnt_storage`. Maybe that should be a parameter to this new function so the caller can tell it about this state.
> 
> Anyway, all that to say, I'm OK with waiting on implementing this behaviour until after my AgX update PR has been merged, since that will add some of the plumbing that will likely be used to implement this Reinhard behaviour.

I agree that this is likely a better fit for the AgX update PR, in the spirit of trying to avoid too many changes in this PR to the underlying infrastructure of the tonemapper.

As for whether HDR is enabled, the viewport can tell during its update loop, which is currently being used to set the max value for the tonemapper. This could also be used to indicate if we are tonemapping to an "HDR range".

> The main API on the linux side is all good, only thing i have a question about is what the purpose of `screen_get_max_full_frame_luminance` is. There's no window variant of this method which could be perfectly fine but since it's unused internally I don't know if it is important enough to need it like `is_hdr_output_supported` did.

It's mostly there to enable game devs to understand the difference in brightness capability in the display when the entire display surface is at a "max value" vs a small point. OLED displays in particular have a limitation in how bright they can get the more of their surface area is lit up, forcing the display to dim the brightest points.

Godot's automatic Max Luminance adjustment does not take this into account currently.

body:
> In Microsoft's documentation, this is described as the difference between display-referred brightness vs scene-referred brightness. SDR display modes seem to always be display-referred.

Just for the record, that's nonsense. Someone messed up when writing that documentation. HDR in Windows is display-referred, just like SDR. The only special thing about it is that it's "absolute" vs. relative like SDR (and HDR on not-Windows).

Scene-referred means that the values correspond to the luminance that would be measured by a sensor / camera in the scene. It's something you basically can't show on a display and would need to go through a mastering process first. In other words, it's before any sort of tone mapping or exposure adjustment happens.

Display-referred means that the values correspond to what you want to show on a particular display, usually the mastering display (in the case of video) or the one of the end user. Iow, everything after tone mapping.

body:
Edit: please disregard this comment as I rework it. (See my [later comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3085668217) for why.)

~~I believe that `RenderingDeviceCommons::ColorSpace` should be renamed to `RenderingDeviceCommons::TransferFunction`.~~

~~Would you mind reviewing and merging this @DarkKilauea? I've also made an adjustment to the data format to make the function name more consistent with the existing `enum` constants.~~

For an explanation why this is necessary: The term "colour space" is often used to describe a **combination** of the following (examples are those that may be used by Godot):

Transfer function (gamma):
- Linear
- Nonlinear sRGB piecewise
- Nonlinear ST2084

Data format (DATA_FORMAT):
- 16 bit floating point per channel (R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT)
- 10-bit uint per channel, 2-bit for alpha (A2R10G10B10_UNORM_PACK32)
- 8-bit uint per channel (R8G8B8A8_UNORM)
- etc.

Colour primaries (gamut):
- sRGB (a.k.a. BT.709)
- P3
- BT.2020

Currently, Godot assumes sRGB colour primaries and a D65 white point. The white point won't change and I believe different colour primaries should be [handled as an entirely separate concept](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12783) from the transfer function and data format in Godot.

~~Because we already have the existing `DATA_FORMAT`, it does not make sense to describe the transfer function as `COLOR_SPACE`.~~
author: allenwp

body:
I am not opposed to *splitting* colorspace into primaries + colorspace but maybe dropping primaries entirely seems a bit too much even if a public wide color gamuts API should be handled in a separate PR. Wayland requires primaries + transfer function metadata to function correctly which is currently implemented in a hacky way (effectively the logic from `_determine_swap_chain_format` is duplicated into the display server) and dropping primaries from the internal API guarantees the logic needs to be duplicated.

That wayland has the color management API be independent of Vulkan also means that the colorspace being determined in the rendering driver (and `prefer_high_precision`) is slightly problematic anyway too. I am aware I could use `screen_get_colorspace` but because of dirty flags I don't believe I have a way to always have correct metadata without polling.

body:
I've taken a bit more of a look into the Vulkan-only issue where HDMI output is reported to be fully supported (according to `DisplayServerWindows::screen_is_hdr_supported` and other functions), but fails to output HDR with the warning:
```
HDR output requested but no HDR compatible format was found, falling back to SDR.
```

This issue occurs consistently for me if I have my display connected to my IGPU (AMD or Intel), but Godot is rendering through my DGPU (NIVIDA PIC-E). If I disable my NVIDIA DGPU entirely, this resolves the problem.

If I debug Godot, I find that it's detecting these Vulkan surface formats and colour spaces:
```
{format=VK_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM (0x0000002c) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_SRGB (0x00000032) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM (0x00000025) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_SRGB (0x0000002b) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_A2B10G10R10_UNORM_PACK32 (0x00000040) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
```

Which match what is expected based on `vulkaninfo`, which gives me [these results](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21394791/vulkan.txt).

And if I disable NVIDIA, I get these formats, which again match  vulkaninfo for the IGU:

```
{format=VK_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_UNORM (0x0000002c) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_B8G8R8A8_SRGB (0x00000032) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_UNORM (0x00000025) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_R8G8B8A8_SRGB (0x0000002b) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_SRGB_NONLINEAR_KHR (0x00000000) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT (0x00000061) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_HDR10_ST2084_EXT (0x3b9c6048) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
{format=VK_FORMAT_A2R10G10B10_UNORM_PACK32 (0x0000003a) colorSpace=VK_COLOR_SPACE_HDR10_ST2084_EXT (0x3b9c6048) }	VkSurfaceFormatKHR
```

So I don't really see a way around this, besides using Vulkan APIs to determine if HDR output is supported instead. The current approach of using `DXGI_OUTPUT_DESC1` simply can't work reliably because the surface formats that Vulkan may or may not support are not guaranteed to match  the DXGI capabilities.

It might make sense to move the `screen_is_hdr_supported` function out of `DisplayServerWindows` and into the driver? I'm really not sure; I haven't actually looked into whether this makes sense, especially in the context of one day having Vulkan use a DXGI swapchain.
author: allenwp

body:
It seems pretty clear to me that the current Vulkan HDR output implementation can not and will not ever allow for HDR output in some configurations when Windows desktop has HDR output enabled and Godot with the D3D12 driver is able to output HDR without issue.

Based on comments from others and my previous comment, this issue may be resolved by using a DXGI swap chain with Vulkan.

Is this Vulkan-only HDR output behaviour even releasable? If we do release this, I suspect the result is that developers may ship a game with Vulkan HDR output because it works fine on their computer. And then they will have players report to them that "HDR output is working great on Windows, but it doesn't work with your game."

To me, this sounds like it might be a substantial enough "foot gun" to developers that we might need to fully disable Windows Vulkan HDR output for the initial release and re-enable it when we have a DXGI swap chain or when GPU drivers better support Vulkan HDR formats in all cases.

Thoughts?
author: allenwp

body:
> Based on comments from others and my previous comment, this issue may be resolved by using a DXGI swap chain with Vulkan.

As far as I know, all HDR-supporting Windows Vulkan games out there use a DXGI swapchain for presesntation. It's a *de facto* requirement at this point. Therefore, I would say it's reasonable to leave out Vulkan support until support for presenting through DXGI is added.

Going forward with https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12234 would also make implementing Vulkan HDR support in Windows less important, as Vulkan on Windows would become a non-default render path.

I've noticed with my laptop (AMD Ryzen™ AI 9 HX 370) that the integrated graphics claim on Vulkan full support for pretty much all the HDR format when the display is an SDR only display. The HDR10->SDR conversion then has some issues with colors looking washed out, where the scRGB color space does not.

Considering all of these issues with Vulkan on Windows, I'm considering disabling the assumption that HDR is always available for Vulkan only builds on Windows and requiring a build with D3D to use HDR. HDR would only be offered if DirectX says that HDR is available, which seems to work correctly on every device I've tested.

I'm not confident in moving the check to the RenderingDevice, because of the behavior of my laptop. It would claim to have HDR support at all times, no matter the attached display. Unfortunately, determining if HDR is available is a combination of graphics driver/API support, Godot support, display support, and OS/Compositor support. I could try to add a check for the correct swap chain support. Which Vulkan this is easier since there is a dedicated API to get the surface formats, but it is harder with DirectX due to when you can actually query the support.

body:
> It might make sense to move the screen_is_hdr_supported function out of DisplayServerWindows and into the driver? I'm really not sure; I haven't actually looked into whether this makes sense, especially in the context of one day having Vulkan use a DXGI swapchain.

I had forgotten to note, absolutely this cannot be the case. On linux I expect modern vulkan drivers to support close to if not all combinations of data format + colorspace (which is what my driver reports). I believe the only check the driver does is whether the *GPU* is capable of doing HDR or not regardless of what the screen is actually capable of. It could be useful to query that the driver is able to perform HDR rendering inside the DisplayServer but it should still always be in the display server.

The check we actually perform under wayland is whether the compositor supports the `wp-color-management` protocol but vulkan is under no obligation to limit its supported formats to those the compositor supports.

What *could* work is adding an API to query the colorspaces the driver supports. For wayland I expect this wouldn't be very helpful but could help with vulkan hdr on windows. But even then it seems vulkan hdr is broken even when the driver claims support for the colorspace. I would agree with disabling support for hdr on vulkan on windows until we can use DXGI swapchains with vulkan.

On a different note, the wayland pr seems to work now (I haven't gotten any reports from someone with an hdr screen yet but it's not broken on my monitor) because I have added a hack to the vulkan driver to use `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT`. This hack works and allows sending HDR metadata to the compositor (sending metadata is handled entirely in the display server) but would break any other users of the vulkan driver. I am not sure what the best API to "disable" using a real colorspace would be but from the changes I've made simply caching the godot equivalent of the colorspace and using that in `get_swapchain_colorspace` seemed to have the correct behaviour.
author: ArchercatNEO

body:
> On linux I expect modern vulkan drivers to support close to if not all combinations of data format + colorspace (which is what my driver reports). I believe the only check the driver does is whether the GPU is capable of doing HDR or not regardless of what the screen is actually capable of.

It's (at least supposed to be) the same on Windows - Vulkan simply doesn't have any API to query display or window capabilities (yet), it can only tell you which formats the driver supports for rendering and displaying. You're expected to use platform-specific APIs for finding out which ones make sense to use.

> COLOR_SPACE_REC709_NONLINEAR_SRGB,

> ```

author: DarkKilauea

body:
As the wayland pr person I should probably comment on the things allenwp discussed. 

> Vulkan swapchain doesn't work on Intel IGPU. Probably simply need to disable HDR output support entirely for Vulkan driver until a DXGI swapchain is implemented for the Vulkan driver https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3133665808

*On windows*. The only driver wayland can use for HDR output is vulkan so it must still support HDR. I hope this isn't news but I feel it's worth clarifing that the *Windows* display server shouldn't support HDR when compiling without D3D12 or when using the vulkan driver and that HDR still needs to be implemented in vulkan.

> It seems that on Windows 10-bit ST2084 ("low precision") should always be preferred because it seems to always be faster and none of us have been able to test with a 12-bit ST2084, HLG, or Dolby Vision hardware output that I'm aware of. Because of this, it probably makes sense to remove public facing API for prefer_high_precision (and maybe even remove the internals for this setting entirely). This way each platform can use whatever format makes most sense and the user doesn't need to have an immensely vast knowledge of HDR to make a good decision on a project setting.

Quick note that on my system (wayland + "hdr" monitor) high precision was always faster than low precision so simply enforcing HDR10 isn't as viable an option. Setting the colorspace from the DisplayServer (as it seems this comment supports) would be preferrable in wayland anyway. The compositor will explicitly tell us what the colorspace it would be most efficient to render in is and therefore being able to set it from within the DisplayServer would be helpful. For some reason though using high precision was always faster on my system despite the compositor recommending HDR10. Perhaps it's an implementation bug somewhere or maybe a problem with my monitor but regardless `prefer_high_precision` didn't make much sense as a setting under wayland either.

(from calinou)
> Reference Luminance can be decreased all the way to 0, which makes the editor unusable as it also affects 2D elements. Here, the editor is behind the popup, but it can't be seen since it's pure black:

The Wayland implementation doesn't allow manually setting reference/maximum luminance so this issue is not applicable specifically to wayland.

And now for some wayland-specific things that required me to modify the Vulkan driver in my PR (which is obviously not ideal)

* `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT`. If this colorspace is not used with the current version of my PR godot will crash from a compositor error. I am not sure what the best approach to using this would be since it would require additions to the driver API to conditionally use a real colorspace (and even just checking if wayland is enabled doesn't work. The compositor may not have implemented the `color-management` protocol). The approach I took was to brick all other users of the vulkan driver and always use `VK_COLOR_SPACE_PASS_THROUGH_EXT`.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/cb1c09ddd1f792c85a00df4808e1b87e898ea1de/drivers/vulkan/rendering_device_driver_vulkan.cpp#L3265-L3282


* `RendererCompositorRD::_compute_reference_multiplier`. As allenwp already mentioned it may be worth pulling this method into the DisplayServer. Thankfully the change I required here was not as severe as the colorspace one: I needed to add a parameter and another conditional branch to the method. https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3074212756

Finally a small note from me.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3085026676. If HDR is enabled in project settings but the DisplayServer doesn't support HDR no warning will ever get logged. This is an issue on linux because for now X11 is the default display server which can't support HDR. This understandably confused calinou on why hdr wasn't working despite running my pr. It would be worth logging a warning if hdr is enabled in project settings but the display server doesn't support it to hopefully reduce the chances of this X11/Wayland confusion.
author: ArchercatNEO

body:
> > @DarkKilauea regarding `enum RD::ColorSpace`: What do you think about adjusting these constants to be the following instead?
> > ```
> > COLOR_SPACE_REC709_LINEAR,
> > COLOR_SPACE_REC709_NONLINEAR_SRGB,
> > COLOR_SPACE_REC2020_NONLINEAR_ST2084,
> > ```
> 
> Makes sense to me, I modeled it off the Vulkan enum since I didn't have anything else at the time. I've made the change with a small tweak, each enum value follows the form `COLOR_SPACE_<primaries>_<transfer_function>`. I dropped the "NONLINEAR` portion since it seems redundant.
> 
> This change has been applied to the latest rebase,

Thanks! I intentionally added the `NONLINEAR` part to help distinguish the transfer function from the primaries to users who are glancing at the enum constants for the first time. This is specifically a concern to me with the following:

```
COLOR_SPACE_P3_SRGB
```
vs.
```
COLOR_SPACE_P3_NONLINEAR_SRGB
```

I expect `COLOR_SPACE_P3_SRGB` will be more confusing than `COLOR_SPACE_P3_NONLINEAR_SRGB`, so I opted to add in the "nonlinear" to denote transfer function. I don't mean to say it's a perfect solution, but I'm very hesitant to go with a convention that will result in `COLOR_SPACE_P3_SRGB` being one of the options because I imagine a user having the first thought of: "What? Is it P3 or sRGB? How is it both?"

Maybe there's a better way to denote that the final part of the constant is a transfer function than inserting `NONLINEAR`... DXGI seems to use `G_`, but "gamma" is an out of date term that implies colour rendering, rather than purely transfer function. We could have `TF_`, but personally I find the full `NONLINEAR` to be the best option given how it aligns nicely to the `COLOR_SPACE_XXX_LINEAR` constants.

**Edit:** Also, would you mind merging in the documentation changes from [my patch/branch](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3132875154)? I used the full "Rec. ITU-R BT.709" format to describe primaries in the docs to ensure there isn't confusion over "Rec. 709" vs. "BT.709" (They're literally the exact same thing, but people get confused by articles that bounce back and forth between the two abbreviations. The full and proper "Rec. ITU-R BT.709" name allows someone who expects "Rec." or "BT." to understand.)

body:
**Oct 24 EDIT:** I can no longer reproduce these issues! I think things were resolved when prefer low precision mode was removed.

I figured out an MRP for the washed out editor window with the d3d12 driver:

**Method 1:**

1. Change rendering driver to d3d12
2. Enable HDR output
3. Make sure Prefer high precision is disabled
4. **Set vsync mode to "Disabled"**
5. Restart the editor

To resolve the issue: Simply set vsync to enabled **or** enable prefer high precision.

MRP: [vsync-washed-out-editor.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/21550955/vsync-washed-out-editor.zip)

**Method 2:**

1. Change rendering driver to d3d12
2. Enable HDR output
3. Make sure Prefer high precision is disabled
4. Restart the editor
5. Close the editor
6. Delete the `.godot/imported` folder
7. Open the project

MRP: [d-3d-12-washed-out-editor.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/22304087/d-3d-12-washed-out-editor.zip)

With this second method, any time HDR output is toggled off and on or prefer high precision is turned on, the issue will be resolved. Restarting the editor also resolves this issue. This issue does not occur when Prefer high precision is enabled.

**Hypothesis**

This issue has a similar visual appearance to [this issue](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3113625898), so it might be that the editor's swapchain buffer is actually an SDR buffer instead of an HDR one.

Because deleting the `.godot/imported` folder seems to cause the bug to occur, even when vysnc is enabled, this is likely an issue that can be caused by having certain editor windows popping up.

body:
> > Test more to verify that high precision is always slower. [#94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3008921107)
> 
> Calinou has recently tested this on macos [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/106814#pullrequestreview-3097412443). The results have been very different mainly due to performance depending on window size. When maximised high precision is faster (though not significantly) and when windowed _somehow_ low precision hdr is _faster_ than sdr by about ~2x. Further testing on macos would definitely be helpful but it seems for optimal performance we definitely require being able to set colorspace at runtime (rather than simply hardcoding a different one for each platform with `#define`s).

I suspect the tradeoff is in several places, which makes the decision to pick high precision or not for a platform a non-trivial decision. Higher precision requires more memory bandwidth, but less operations in the blit shader (though a compositor may have its own operations to convert to the monitor's format). Lower precision is less bandwidth, but requires more operations.

As a result, I'm in agreement that we shouldn't remove the ability for the gamedev (or end user) to set the precision mode (as proposed earlier in the comments), it may have significant impact based on the OS, window manager, and game.

> There are also several fidelity issues but given that the PR hasn't been rebased in a while I would wait until it is before coming to any conclusions about possible bugs in the vulkan driver.

Should be rebased now, sorry for the delay.
