body:
Got some time this weekend to read through everyone's comments, thanks for the input!

> Issues:
> 
>     * Mobile HDR output should work up to values of 2.0. Did we ever figure this out? Last I heard mention of it was: [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-2611708189)

The format of R10G10B10A2 in the mobile renderer really limits the final dynamic range in a way that makes HDR output basically useless. I'm waiting for a PR from @clayjohn that changes the mobile renderer to use a full 16 bit color buffer for mobile when `hdr_2d` is enabled. That should make this squashing of the dynamic range no longer necessary.

>     * Vulkan swapchain doesn't work on Intel integreated GPU. Vulkan swapchain also doesn't work with NVIDIA GPU drivers via integrated GPU (Intel or AMD) HDMI port hardware. Probably simply need to disable HDR output support entirely for Vulkan driver until a DXGI swapchain is implemented for the Vulkan driver [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3133665808)

Couldn't we place a warning in the documentation instead? It seems pretty extreme to shut off the feature for the de-facto primary renderer in Godot, if the errors only arise if you plug into a port that isn't from your graphics card. As I understand it, the common advice for PC builders is to always plug into the dedicated graphics card to avoid issues with games.

I am thinking of dropping support for Vulkan only builds in Windows due to the need for DirectX to get critical information about the display for HDR. I'll probably do that soon.

>     * Compatibility throws a bunch of errors with my test project that are not thrown in Mobile/Forward+. Need to look into these.

Looks like your test project made some assumptions about the existence of a `RenderingDevice` which don't hold when the capability renderer is used. I've made a branch with fixes here: https://github.com/DarkKilauea/godot-hdr-output-test-project/tree/fix-compatibility

>     * `get_window().hdr_output_reference_luminance` does not update immediately, so when you change the SDR Content Brightness Windows setting, Godot doesn't update until you resize/move the game window or something similar. (Issue 3 in [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-2761720109) )
>       
>       * If there's no "zero performance cost" option to solve this, then it's OK to leave this behaviour. If there is a Windows notification we can subscribe to, that would be ideal.

In my testing project, I see the `SDR White Level` meter change in real time, but I am noticing that the reference brightness isn't actually changing. This is probably a bug, I'll chase it down.

>     * D3212 editor window appears washed out when vsync is disabled (still happens as of Aug 1): [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3144969331)

I can reproduce this on my NVidia GPU, so there might be a bug here. Adding it to the list.

>     * If the display server doesn't support HDR but HDR is enabled in project settings no warning will be logged: [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3085026676)

I set it up this way intentionally to avoid errors in the editor when it is opened on a display that didn't support HDR. I'm viewing the project setting as more of a "please turn on HDR if you can", than something that should error if HDR couldn't actually be enabled. Trying to enable HDR via the API does error (if the request could never be honored), since the developer probably wants to know their operation didn't take place.

>     * Boot screen background colour must be converted to linear when HDR output is enabled: [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#discussion_r2248750183)

I got worse results when I tried to do this, the color came out way too dark. I'm thinking something in the renderer is converting from sRGB itself, or the blit shader is already performing an sRGB to linear conversion.

>     * Has all feedback raised by Calinou been addressed? [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (review)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#pullrequestreview-3007094400)

Not yet, this is what I know so far:

>> I get a crash on startup when using D3D12 (even if HDR is disabled), but Vulkan works. The crash also happens on master, so it must be due to some configuration issue or outdated dependencies on my end.

I cannot reproduce this on my machine, Since it happens on master, either we have a bug unrelated to this PR, or there is a local issue.

>> Reference Luminance can be decreased all the way to 0, which makes the editor unusable as it also affects 2D elements.

Agree that the project settings and window settings should have lower limits. Maybe should be the lowest here for reference since it matches the reference for sRGB? Adding it to the list.

>> Project Settings only apply to the main editor window, not to its popups like the Project Settings.

I'm not sure what to do about this one. Each window is completely independent and the project settings only affect the "main window". Should windows inherit the HDR settings from their parents? They do when sub-windows are embedded to prevent around bugs within game UI.

>> SMAA has broken artifacts on bright surfaces when HDR is enabled.

Adding to the list.

>     * Has "Should update screen_use_luminance logic to fallback to a default if this method returns 0" been resolved? [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#discussion_r2072918814)
>       
>       * I think it has been resolved, as seen in the `DisplayServerWindows::_update_hdr_output_for_window` function.

This should be resolved.

> API Review:
> 
>     * A big API review probably needed in dedicated rendering meeting at some point to make sure we are minimizing bloat/maintenance to only the necessary API surface.

Yes, we need to pick a date and time that works for everyone. I'll follow up on the contributor's chat.

>     * Screen luminance functions return 0 when they can't get that information. Is this the best way to handle this? Some platforms don't give certain information at all; would it be good to have a different API that makes it clear whether the request for screen info was successful or not? It seems that 0 is used as a magic number in `DisplayServerWindows::_update_hdr_output_for_window` to tell if screen info was successfully retrieved.

I went with 0 since it isn't a value you'd actually want to use, but is less likely to break anything than a negative number if passed down the stack. However, if folks think a negative value should denote failures, I'm happy to do so with some additional guards.

>     * I don't think there is value for the "tonemap to window" project setting, so it might make sense to remove this project setting entirely and leave it as only a viewport property?

A usage I could think of is someone that wants to output colors, say in 2D, that are brighter than `1.0`, but didn't want tonemapping to use that additional range. This is pretty niche and I wouldn't be opposed to removing the setting.

>     * allenwp TODO: really play around with "tonemap to window" to see when a user might want to disable this feature. It's possible that this API might need to be hidden/removed until a proposal with a real-world use case can inform exactly how the API should be designed(???)

The API is needed for folks that want to use viewports for special effects, like rendering heightmaps or cloud textures, and don't want any chance a tonemapper could interfere with those values. The default for this setting is off for that reason, to maintain compatibility with existing viewports that are not meant for direct display.

>     * `get_hdr_output_max_value` might be better named `get_output_max_value` to make it clear that this is the `output_max_value` independent of whether HDR is enabled in the project. (Current name has advantage of discoverability due to being named similar as other HDR functions, but has disadvantage of suggesting that this output value is only valid when HDR output is active.)

I'm on the same fence, I like that it is grouped with the rest of the HDR output functionality, but it could apply to other use cases. However, the value is always going to be `1.0` in SDR scenarios, it really isn't that useful outside of games targeting HDR displays.

>     * How should we deal with SDR screen info values when HDR output is disabled? [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3063115023)

I don't think providing the actual screen capabilities really hurts anything and it simplifies understanding the API. Otherwise, folks need to keep in mind an edge case where you cannot get screen brightness info outside of HDR displays or the HDR output mode.

As far as SDR content authorship is concerned, the brightness of the display is meaningless, `1.0` will be mapped to the target brightness by the OS. But, maybe some indie developer wants to do something fun with the screen's max brightness in relation to their reference display.

> 
> Documentation:
> 
>     * I haven't reviewed documentation in months and it makes sense to wait until the API is finalized before looking at this.
> 
>     * Max Luminance is ignored by Linear tonemapper, so it should be noted that this is the case.

The current documentation implies that, but I agree it could be made more clear. I'll add a note.

body:
> I set it up this way intentionally to avoid errors in the editor when it is opened on a display that didn't support HDR. I'm viewing the project setting as more of a "please turn on HDR if you can", than something that should error if HDR couldn't actually be enabled. Trying to enable HDR via the API does error (if the request could never be honored), since the developer probably wants to know their operation didn't take place.

I brought this up because of @Calinou anyway so they should probably have some say in this. I wasn't thinking that if the physical screen/window doesn't support HDR a warning should be logged (that would raise an immense amount of useless warnings) but only if the display server doesn't. That way when someone opens Godot using X11 they will get a warning saying the X11 display server doesn't support HDR instead of wondering why their HDR isn't working.

> I suspect the tradeoff is in several places, which makes the decision to pick high precision or not for a platform a non-trivial decision. Higher precision requires more memory bandwidth, but less operations in the blit shader (though a compositor may have its own operations to convert to the monitor's format). Lower precision is less bandwidth, but requires more operations.

Something I wondered is why is the API limited to high/low precision only? I am aware we do not support P3 yet but couldn't prefer high precision be `window_set_colorspace` or something like that? It would mean less API changes if we ever decide to implement P3.
author: ArchercatNEO

body:
> I brought this up because of @Calinou anyway so they should probably have some say in this. I wasn't thinking that if the physical screen/window doesn't support HDR a warning should be logged (that would raise an immense amount of useless warnings) but only if the display server doesn't. That way when someone opens Godot using X11 they will get a warning saying the X11 display server doesn't support HDR instead of wondering why their HDR isn't working.

I am 50/50 on this issue. When you work on a project's visual aspects, you want everyone to be using HDR if possible, but this is not possible in all scenarios (e.g. not everyone in the team may be using HDR-ready monitors, let alone ones with good HDR).

If you regularly toggle HDR on your PC, you may not always realize that you left it in SDR mode when opening a project that's meant to be iterated upon with HDR enabled. This has happened to me several times when launching games on Windows, since you don't want HDR to always be enabled on Windows due to subpar SDR content presentation. On this account, it fully makes sense to warn users in the editor when HDR is enabled in the project settings but isn't actually engaged because it's turned off at an OS level. On the other hand, the warning when HDR is not supported at the OS/display server level is probably not needed, since you can't toggle HDR at the system level there (e.g. Linux/X11).

From this artist perspective, you'll probably want a way to quickly toggle between HDR and SDR, since not all of your players will be playing in HDR. However, keep in mind that SDR presentation on HDR is not great on Windows (and passable on Linux), while macOS handles it much better. To get an accurate SDR presentation, you would need to not only disable HDR in the engine, but also in the OS/monitor, which implies modesetting (and therefore a several-second long flicker).

From a player perspective, the warning is probably unneeded. As long as there's a way to query in advance if HDR is supported by the OS and monitor (according to OS APIs), options menus can easily disable the HDR checkbox.

The default for this setting is off for that reason, to maintain compatibility with existing viewports that are not meant for direct display.

> > ```
> > * `get_hdr_output_max_value` might be better named `get_output_max_value` to make it clear that this is the `output_max_value` independent of whether HDR is enabled in the project. (Current name has advantage of discoverability due to being named similar as other HDR functions, but has disadvantage of suggesting that this output value is only valid when HDR output is active.)
> > ```
> 
> I'm on the same fence, I like that it is grouped with the rest of the HDR output functionality, but it could apply to other use cases. However, the value is always going to be `1.0` in SDR scenarios, it really isn't that useful outside of games targeting HDR displays.

With the current name: if I were to use the function without looking at the documentation I would expect that it is only useful when targeting HDR displays, so I would write code like this:

```
var max_output: float = 1.0
if window.hdr_output_enabled:
	max_output = window.get_hdr_output_max_value()
```

But this circumvents the entire convenience of the function. I expect this function to be used by plugins on the Asset Store, so those authors should be encouraged to use this function even if they aren't thinking about HDR output and aren't looking at any of the HDR functions.

So that makes me lean towards `get_output_max_value`.

Now that I'm thinking about plugins from authors who don't know much about HDR, this function could also be paired with a `get_output_max_full_frame_value` which would return either `1.0` or `screen_get_max_full_frame_luminance / hdr_output_reference_luminance` if `screen_get_max_full_frame_luminance` has been successfully read from the screen...

> > ```
> > * How should we deal with SDR screen info values when HDR output is disabled? [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3063115023)
> > ```
> 
> I don't think providing the actual screen capabilities really hurts anything and it simplifies understanding the API. Otherwise, folks need to keep in mind an edge case where you cannot get screen brightness info outside of HDR displays or the HDR output mode.
> 
> As far as SDR content authorship is concerned, the brightness of the display is meaningless, `1.0` will be mapped to the target brightness by the OS. But, maybe some indie developer wants to do something fun with the screen's max brightness in relation to their reference display.

Hmm. The issue here is that reference, max, and max full frame luminance values should always be equal in SDR. It doesn't matter which we pick, but having them not equal goes against the paradigm used in HDR and causes the "simplified API" to actually become complex to use since it results in very different behaviour based on HDR or SDR output. So maybe when outputting SDR we should return max luminance for all three values to allow the user to do something with what Windows provides as max luminance (even though that's probably always going to be exactly 270.0).

body:
Turns out the Staples that is a 3 min walk from my house has a demo laptop with a built in HDR display. Unfortunately, they don't have a laptop with an HDR display and dedicated GPU, but I was still able to get some good testing done. The laptop is an Asus Zenbook UX3402VA.

### HDR with Intel integrated graphics

The same issue [described here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3113625898) occurs: HDR supposedly fully supported according to Godot, but it is actually an SDR nonlinear sRGB swapchain. This produces a grey washed out image. I don't see how this is fixable; it seems that it is a common issue with modern Intel GPU drivers. D3D12 driver with HDR works without issue.

### Laptop display brightness and windows HDR content brightness

The laptop display brightness setting appears to adjust all luminance properties of the display (min, max, and full frame max) and does **not** affect the SDR white level (reference luminance). This is expected and means that we should be polling for (or subscribing to?) display information regularly to ensure that games reasonably quickly respond to laptop display brightness settings.

It seems that the HDR content brightness user setting **replaces SDR content brightness user setting** in the Windows display settings. HDR content brightness behaves similar to SDR content brightness: it changes the SDR white level. **Additionally**, the HDR content brightness user setting adjusts the other luminance properties (min, max, and full frame max).

Here is a google drive link that has a video recording of the behaviour: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1PAvLdTsUAONUXPPwT4TVA27WsIrmqhXP?usp=sharing

I have also included a screenshot of what the luminance values look like when the brightness and HDR content brightness are both turned down to zero:

- max luminance: 49,353.55 nits
- max full frame luminance: 32,000 nits
- SDR white level: 80 nits

From simply looking at the display I can confirm that the SDR white level was easily less than 40 nits: it was so dark I basically couldn't see the display anymore. So the 80 nits SDR white level is incorrect. Additionally, my eyes were not being destroyed by an insanely bright 50,000 nits from this cheap consumer grade OLED display, so obviously that value is entirely wrong as well.

Conversely, the values actually were all very reasonable when the brightness of the laptop was turned up to maximum brightness:
- max luminance: 759.29 nits
- max full frame luminance: 492.31 nits
- SDR white level: 480 nits

### Takeaway

Thankfully there isn't too much we need to change to deal with this.

Because Windows doesn't seem to scale SDR White Level to be lower than 80, even when the display is clearly much darker, it means that we need to be able to support maximum luminance values that are much brighter than physically reasonable when "auto adjust max luminance" is enabled. I need to think about what the cap should be, but maybe it should be uncapped. This display went *very* dark, even darker than the 48 nits cinema reference luminance...

body:
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/102987#issuecomment-3321782567
> > > iOS and Android will also not support changing max luminance or reference luminance. We need to figure out how to properly expose this difference in the API...
> > 
> > 
> > Is there any platform other than Windows which truly requires calibrating anything in-game rather than relying on the OS-provided data being correct?
> 
> This is expected for Mac OS when connected to an external monitor or TV. Pretty much anything that can be connected to an external TV needs to have some way of setting max luminance.

This made me think, what should the behaviour of auto adjust luminance be when the window is projected on multiple screens?

If the window is only ever on the external TV screen then hopefully the existing metadata is sufficient but if the window is on multiple ones godot will only ever report *one* of them. Is this even a supported mode for auto adjust luminance or enough of an edge case it won't be supported?
author: ArchercatNEO

body:
> This made me think, what should the behaviour of auto adjust luminance be when the window is projected on multiple screens?
> 
> If the window is only ever on the external TV screen then hopefully the existing metadata is sufficient but if the window is on multiple ones godot will only ever report _one_ of them. Is this even a supported mode for auto adjust luminance or enough of an edge case it won't be supported?

I believe that it is convention that any time a window is between screens, it will use all of the metadata from the screen that the largest portion of the window is a part of and colour will be simply incorrect on the other screen that holds a minority of the window. This has been the case in the Windows operating system for a long time, even before HDR. It happens with DPI scaling and also with ICC colour profiles.

body:
> > ```
> > * `get_hdr_output_max_value` might be better named `get_output_max_value` to make it clear that this is the `output_max_value` independent of whether HDR is enabled in the project. (Current name has advantage of discoverability due to being named similar as other HDR functions, but has disadvantage of suggesting that this output value is only valid when HDR output is active.)
> > ```
> 
> 
> I'm on the same fence, I like that it is grouped with the rest of the HDR output functionality, but it could apply to other use cases. However, the value is always going to be `1.0` in SDR scenarios, it really isn't that useful outside of games targeting HDR displays.

I feel quite strongly that we should use `get_output_max_value` instead of assigning this method the `_hdr` prefix. My reason is that I believe it is a bug for plugins to hardcode `1.0` values into their code when they intend to use the `Window`'s `output_max_value`. Because this method does the switching between SDR and HDR automatically, the developer really doesn't need to know or care about HDR; they just use this method to get the current output max value and it will work well with projects that target SDR or HDR output.

I've pushed a commit to make this change that also consolidates the logic for this HDR and SDR switching to the `RenderingContextDriver` so that each `DisplayServer` doesn't need to re-implement the same logic. If this can be moved even further up to the `RenderingServer` base class, that would be even better, but I didn't immediately see a way to do that.

I also renamed `screen_get_sdr_white_level` to `screen_get_reference_luminance`; "SDR white level" is primarily a Windows term, so it should be made consistent with the rest of the Godot public facing API and use "reference luminance" instead.

Documentation still needs an update, but I'll do that in a separate pass.

Regarding `tonemap_to_window`, I think this would be much better suited as an `enum`: `tonemap_range` with values `Window` (uses `Window.get_output_max_value`) and `SDR` (uses `1.0`). This gives a lot more flexibility in the long run if we ever add a third option, such as `custom` or maybe even something like `Window_full_frame`. I'll start work on this change next.

body:
> > ```
> > * Screen luminance functions return 0 when they can't get that information. Is this the best way to handle this? Some platforms don't give certain information at all; would it be good to have a different API that makes it clear whether the request for screen info was successful or not? It seems that 0 is used as a magic number in `DisplayServerWindows::_update_hdr_output_for_window` to tell if screen info was successfully retrieved.
> > ```
> 
> 
> I went with 0 since it isn't a value you'd actually want to use, but is less likely to break anything than a negative number if passed down the stack. However, if folks think a negative value should denote failures, I'm happy to do so with some additional guards.

> > ```
> > * How should we deal with SDR screen info values when HDR output is disabled? [[Windows] Support output to HDR monitors #94496 (comment)](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3063115023)
> > ```
> 
> 
> I don't think providing the actual screen capabilities really hurts anything and it simplifies understanding the API. Otherwise, folks need to keep in mind an edge case where you cannot get screen brightness info outside of HDR displays or the HDR output mode.
> 
> As far as SDR content authorship is concerned, the brightness of the display is meaningless, `1.0` will be mapped to the target brightness by the OS. But, maybe some indie developer wants to do something fun with the screen's max brightness in relation to their reference display.

I started a chat in the `#devel` channel of RocketChat regarding how we normally handle methods that may not be able to return a valid value: using a sentinel value, like `0` is a common approach in Godot.

...But given some platforms simply don't even provide this information (Mac OS), or other configurations don't provide this screen luminance information (SDR), I had another thought: This screen information could be provided through the public scripting API as a dictionary. This dictionary will only include the screen luminance information that was able to be correctly retrieved. In some configurations, the dictionary will be empty or partially empty.

Because users will typically be using `Window.get_output_max_value()` (or possibly `Window.get_output_max_full_frame_value()`), this screen luminance information doesn't need to be queried all the time and is mostly for debug or niche use cases.

I believe the internals won't need to change much for this; this proposal is only related to the public scripting API.

> > > ```
> > 
> >

The default for this setting is off for that reason, to maintain compatibility with existing viewports that are not meant for direct display.
> 
> 
> Those do sound like good use cases. I'm pondering if a name like `tonemap_to_sdr` or `force_tonemap_to_sdr` could be more intuitive: a user who is not thinking about HDR output would be confused about what the difference is between tonemapping to the window or not, while `tonemap_to_sdr` makes it more clear that this is specifically relevant to SDR/HDR functionality. (This is logically the opposite, so some code would need to be changed to adopt this name.)

I've thought more about this and I propose removing the `tonemap_to_window` and `tonemap_to_screen` functionality entirely and have the tonemap range determined simply by the `hdr_2d` Viewport setting (`hdr_2d`:  tonemap to window, else: tonemap to SDR). To address the use cases brought up in these previous comments, I propose the following in a separate Proposal and PR instead:

1. A "HDR 2D tonemap range" property added to `Environment` that will have these options:
   - Window
   - SDR
   - (others such as "custom" or "Window full frame max")
2. A "HDR 2D clamp to tonemap range" property added to `Environment` that will clamp to the tonemap range as the very last step of `tonemap.glsl`.

body:
Rebased off the latest master and fixed a few bugs.

- Changes to SDR Content Brightness in Windows will automatically apply to Godot.
    - There is a bit of a delay (500ms) due to the implementation polling the value and checking for changes. Unfortunately, there does not seem to be any message sent to the app from Windows when this value is changed, so polling is the only option.
 - Set 80 nits as the lower value for setting reference and max luminance in project settings and the inspector.
     - This was set to the standard reference brightness for sRGB, which seemed reasonable.
 - Vulkan only builds no longer assume HDR output is available. 
     - There were too many compromises with HDR when running in this mode, so I decided to make DirectX support being compiled in a requirement for HDR output. We can revisit this later if needed.

body:
I have just tried this pr, and it seems to work well! One issue, however, I am experiencing raised shadows. This is not godot specific, as some other programs also have it. (but it may be possible to fix it here.)

When enabling HDR in windows 11 you will immediately notice 2 things: First, all SDR content is less saturated, this is the correct behavior. But then, all SDR content has lifted shadows, this is not normal. This has to do with windows using the wrong gamma to place SDR content in the HDR 'container' for viewing on a HDR screen. This makes SDR content in HDR look really bad on windows. But even worse, somehow, this incorrect gamma also gets applied to _some_ HDR programs! This includes Godot and Blender 5.0. This issue does not exist on Linux (KDE) and MacOS.

One of the programs that does not have this issue is the MPV video player, it only seems to rely on windows to get the max luminance value. It also plays SDR videos correctly as it does its own SDR to HDR conversion. (It always plays it at 203 nits with the correct gamma.)  

There is a somewhat hacky solution for this problem (With a great explanation): https://github.com/dylanraga/win11hdr-srgb-to-gamma2.2-icm has calibration profiles for different windows SDR brightness settings in HDR, and they correct for the wrong gamma. This also has its own problems: the correction does not seem perfect, the profiles have 800 nits max brightness baked in, and programs that have good looking HDR (like MPV) will now look bad. And since this is a modification the user needs to make to windows, not a lot of people will do something like this. 

So to me, the best solution seems to be having Godot circumvent the windows gamma application. (Or at least having the option to do so.) Or is this outside of the scope of this pr?
author: WrobotGames

body:
> When enabling HDR in windows 11 you will immediately notice 2 things: First, all SDR content is less saturated, this is the correct behavior. But then, all SDR content has lifted shadows, this is not normal. This has to do with windows using the wrong gamma to place SDR content in the HDR 'container' for viewing on a HDR screen. This makes SDR content in HDR look really bad on windows. But even worse, somehow, this incorrect gamma also gets applied to _some_ HDR programs! This includes Godot and Blender 5.0. This issue does not exist on Linux (KDE) and MacOS.

This does not match my understanding. I have both a Macbook Pro (2025 model) and a Windows 11 desktop, and I believe both behave identically with SDR content via HDR output when I connect them to the same display; importantly, Mac **displays** are very high quality HDR displays. So often, the difference people see is the difference between an Apple display and some other brand of display. I have an ASUS ProArt OLED PA32UCDM and it produces the same sort of blacks in SDR content via HDR that I get with my Macbook display, regardless of whether I connect it to my Windows PC or Macbook.

> One of the programs that does not have this issue is the MPV video player, it only seems to rely on windows to get the max luminance value. It also plays SDR videos correctly as it does its own SDR to HDR conversion. (It always plays it at 203 nits with the correct gamma.)
> 
> There is a somewhat hacky solution for this problem (With a great explanation): https://github.com/dylanraga/win11hdr-srgb-to-gamma2.2-icm has calibration profiles for different windows SDR brightness settings in HDR, and they correct for the wrong gamma. This also has its own problems: the correction does not seem perfect, the profiles have 800 nits max brightness baked in, and programs that have good looking HDR (like MPV) will now look bad. And since this is a modification the user needs to make to windows, not a lot of people will do something like this.

First off, video files are not normally encoded with sRGB; they use different colour spaces that have defined transforms to other spaces (for better or for worse). This is not my field of expertise, so I can't comment on video decoding specifically.

One could argue that the 2.2 power function vs. inverse nonlinear sRGB (piecewise) transfer function mismatch should be simulated when presenting sRGB content via a different standard, but this is incorrect according to the sRGB standard, which states that the piecewise function should be used to convert to CIE XYZ, which is needed when converting to HDR (I wrote about this on this [blog post](https://allenwp.com/blog/2025/05/06/why-windows-srgb-sdr-over-hdr-is-technically-correct/)). Additionally, and importantly, displays are incapable of correctly displaying very dark values because of viewing flare and other limitations of screen technology.

So over the years, many displays have depended on the 2.2/piecewise mismatch to compensate for the display not being able to correctly render very dark values. With the HDR10 standard, the signal sent to the display is absolute nits values: no compensation for the challenge of rendering very dark values should be included in this signal! So when you see new OLED displays that have a black level adjustment, this is the new feature that the display has to correct for the fact that the display is incapable of displaying very low nits values and replaces the old 2.2/piecewise mismatch used by old and simple monitors with sRGB content.

> So to me, the best solution seems to be having Godot circumvent the windows gamma application. (Or at least having the option to do so.) Or is this outside of the scope of this pr?

Let's say we attempted to correct this issue in Godot while displays are continuing to improve and become better at handling very dark values correctly in HDR signals... Eventually, the image produced by Godot would no longer match the correct image because the new displays are correctly handling the very low nits values by compensating internally. So this approach of simulating the mismatch is simply not future-proofed and is far too dependent on how displays behave, which is changing from year to year.

All this to say, the best thing for Godot to do is to provide the correct values to Windows and Mac OS, which will be correctly passed onto the display. Eventually, it will become normal for displays to have correct black level adjustments built-in for displaying HDR content, so SDR content will look similar via an HDR signal as it did on old monitors that depended on the mismatch.

I will end by saying that my I have an old Asus ProArt SDR/HDR monitor and a new ASUS ProArt OLED PA32UCDM and when the old monitor is running in sRGB mode with 2.2, it looks similar in the blacks in my new OLED monitor when it is presenting SDR content via HDR. This is NOT the case if I were to compare with my old LCD HDR displays. So this does really suggest that displays are continuing to improve and the problem will eventually become uncommon.

> And how come 'calibrated' SDR looks so much different than SDR over HDR? (I would expect it to look the same, or at least close.) 

1) It doesn't look very different when you have a good HDR display that has some black level compensation built in, like the displays on MacBook Pros or my calibrated OLED Asus reference HDR display. I can barely tell the difference with a good modern HDR display, unlike with an old HDR display where it's a radically different image.

author: allenwp

body:
> First off, video files are not normally encoded with sRGB; they use different colour spaces that have defined transforms to other spaces (for better or for worse). This is not my field of expertise, so I can't comment on video decoding specifically.

The situation with SDR videos is very similar to sRGB: BT709 (a piece-wise TF) describes how SDR videos are encoded, and BT1886 (gamma 2.4, more or less) describes how it's decoded.
The difference is that everyone agrees that using the piece-wise TF to display BT709 videos would be nonsense, so the video space doesn't really have this particular problem (as much).

> One could argue that the 2.2 power function vs. inverse nonlinear sRGB (piecewise) transfer function mismatch should be simulated when presenting sRGB content via a different standard, but this is incorrect according to the sRGB standard, which states that the piecewise function should be used to convert to CIE XYZ, which is needed when converting to HDR (I wrote about this on this [blog post](https://allenwp.com/blog/2025/05/06/why-windows-srgb-sdr-over-hdr-is-technically-correct/)). Additionally, and importantly, displays are incapable of correctly displaying very dark values because of viewing flare and other limitations of screen technology.

Converting between standards requires replicating how the signal is displayed on an actual display following the standard, not some hypothetical values that noone has actually ever seen..

Implementing a virtual sRGB display on top of another standard is no different from implementing an sRGB display on the hardware level - the latter translates the 'electrical' signal values to some actual electrical signal (with a different 'transfer function'), which then drives a pixel to achieve some brightness level. The combined transfer function of that is gamma 2.2 for a correct sRGB display.
Showing sRGB content on a non-sRGB display just introduces another conversion step in the pipeline, but the end result has to be the same, or you show an incorrect image.

> So over the years, many displays have depended on the 2.2/piecewise mismatch to compensate for the display not being able to correctly render very dark values. With the HDR10 standard, the signal sent to the display is absolute nits values: no compensation for the challenge of rendering very dark values should be included in this signal! So when you see new OLED displays that have a black level adjustment, this is the new feature that the display has to correct for the fact that the display is incapable of displaying very low nits values and replaces the old 2.2/piecewise mismatch used by old and simple monitors with sRGB content.

That doesn't make sense to me, because
- the mismatch makes low values darker than using piece-wise on the display side. To compensate for flare / get contrast closer to the intended image with bad black levels, you'd need to make them brighter
- displays have always implicitly done black point compensation, both in SDR and HDR mode. That is not a new thing; LCDs just generally got away without sensor-based (or manual) black level adjustment because their black level was high enough to work out well in most real world situations (and still most provide a setting to adjust the black level anyways)
- if more OLEDs now do black level adjustment and end up more similar to LCDs in behavior, shouldn't sRGB content be displayed on them more similar to how it was always displayed on LCDs, instead of arbitrarily different?
- as of today (where Windows HDR is still not *that* common), the vast majority of sRGB content is authored on displays that are gamma 2.2 + BPC. Whatever theoretical calculations is mismatch a standard includes, authors create images to look good on their real world display (which is to say, usually *not* piece-wise)

Having written all this down, I realize this isn't really the right place for this discussion. @WrobotGames maybe an issue for your feature request would be better? I think it's a good idea, both for game creators (that can quickly check how the game will *actually* look on SDR screens, without having to turn off HDR system wide all the time) and for players of games that don't enable HDR for some reason.

body:
Hey folks!

Members of the rendering team and interested parties met on Sunday to discuss the public API of this PR. We decided to reduce the public surface area and simplify the exposed concepts to make it easier to use.

As a result, the following changes have been made:

- Support for outputting the HDR10 format has been dropped in favor of always providing a 16bit linear color signal. This simplifies the implementation and allows the OS/driver to handle conversion to the wire format of the display. There are benefits for compositing as well. All APIs related to `prefer_high_precision` have been removed as a result.
- Restricted luminance settings to the DisplayServer exclusively, removing them from Window and ProjectSettings.
- Removed the `auto_adjust` settings entirely, replacing them with passing negative values to the associated luminance setters to enable auto adjustment. APIs have been added to get the current max and reference luminance of the window.
- Changed the wording of `set_hdr_output_enabled` to `request_hdr_output` to make it more clear that HDR output is a request that can only be honored if all the preconditions are met and may be disabled if those conditions change during runtime.
- Removed all `screen_` methods related to getting display capabilities for HDR. These were not always possible to implement on every OS and aren't strictly necessary to implementing HDR in a game or application.
- Removed methods for getting the color space or format of a window. These were not used outside of diagnostics.
- Removed `tonemap_to_window` and associated properties (thanks @allenwp!)
- Added a warning if HDR output is requested in the project settings, but `hdr_2d` is disabled for the main viewport. HDR 2D will still be turned on automatically if you forget.

Documentation has been updated to explain the changed functionality and new APIs. I don't have an HDR display with me currently (will get back home next week), so I could use some help testing to make sure everything works correctly. I've run sanity checks through all the code paths on my laptop and everything seems to be fine.

Things to do:

- I'm going to dig through the changes related to providing the max output value to the tone mapper to see if we can simplify it.
- It might be possible to simplify the blit shader a bit more and remove the "color space" check. I'm looking for a way to do that which doesn't cause more confusion by adding another "hdr" getter, since that is quite overloaded.

I was able to get some work done today on this PR. Here is the summary:

### Resolved issues

1. Boot screen clear colour was incorrect; I've pushed a fix for this.
2. I can no longer reproduce the issue where the editor is washed out when v-sync is disabled.
3. Vulkan swapchain issues are resovled; **Vulkan driver no longer supports HDR output.**
   - Error/warning reporting is still needed.

### Change `get_output_max_value` to `get_output_max_linear_value`

I've pushed a change to rename this method:

Changing to `get_output_max_linear_value` may help improve usability and correct usage of the function for some users, considering the following:

- All `Color` in Godot is expected to be stored using nonlinear sRGB encoding. (This is explicitly stated in documentation.)
- The primary use case for this method is to scale `Color` to be the brightest that can be displayed on screen.
- Many Godot users are not familiar with the need to perform colour maths on linear values to prevent change in hue.
- Many Godot users do not carefully read and follow documentation.
- Compared to `get_output_max_value` `get_output_max_linear_value` gives an additional hint to Godot users that `Color` must be converted to linear before scaling by this max value.

Additionally, I do not see any significant downside to adding `linear` to the function name; it only slightly increases the length and does not add any ambiguity.

### Remaining issues

- Warnings needed when rendering driver does not support HDR output.
   - If you have "request HDR output" enabled, but are using the Vulkan rendering driver.
- Warnings regarding HDR 2D being needed aren't working correctly just yet.
- Other warnings/error reporting might be helpful...
- SMAA has artifacts: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#pullrequestreview-3007094400

body:
### Default tonemapper in editor

> [dark_kilauea] This one is tricky, since any change will affect how artists see their scenes by default. Basically we are moving back to before 4.0 where tonemapping was not shown by default. Is there a way to offer a Flimic like tonemapping when HDR is enabled, even if it isn’t a perfect match in SDR? Maybe this would be a better approach?

I have very strong feelings that the Filmic tonemapper with a `white` parameter of `1.0` is the incorrect default environment for the 3D workspace. If a tonemapper was provided, its white parameter should be set to `2.0`, not `1.0`. With a `white` of `1.0`, this is simply a contrast curve that has an impact on the colour rendering (hues and saturation of colours) that makes it much more difficult to match colours between your art tools and the Godot editor.

HDR output provides a good prompting to address this existing issue and 4.7 is a great time for this change. The Linear tonemapper is the obvious correct approach because it ensures that colours and hues are not affected within the range that can be displayed by the user's screen and allows full and correct support of HDR output. If users still want the filmic tonemapper with a `white` of `1.0` in their default environment, they can still enable it through the editor quite easily.

If folks believe this change is better in a separate PR, that's fine. I figure it's reasonable to put it in this PR because this is the PR that requires the change. (Without this change the editor cannot correctly render HDR output in the default 3D workspace.)

body:
While working on getting HDR back working on my Android phones (#101977), I learned that Android does not support taking a linear 16bit signal and displaying it with extra headroom, it will treat such a signal as SDR.

In order to get the display to actually emit the additional brightness, you need to send an HDR10, HLG, or Dolby Vision signal.

This challenges our assumption that a 16bit linear signal is sufficient for all platforms. In that PR, I've added back in support for HDR10 behind an `#ifdef ANDROID_ENABLED`, but I wonder if we might need that in other platforms. We may need an internal API to instruct the rendering driver which color spaces it must request in order to enable HDR.
author: DarkKilauea

body:
> This challenges our assumption that a 16bit linear signal is sufficient for all platforms. In that PR, I've added back in support for HDR10 behind an #ifdef ANDROID_ENABLED, but I wonder if we might need that in other platforms. We may need an internal API to instruct the rendering driver which color spaces it must request in order to enable HDR.

Given that https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/12783 is something we may want to implement someday, it seems like adding an internal rendering device driver API to request a particular colorspace could be sufficient for that.

In c++, (only one of these, whichever align better with our goals)
```cpp
void surface_set_colorspace(p_colorspace); // using the colorspace enum
void surface_set_colorspace(p_primaries, p_transfer_function); // using split primaries/tf enums (means less enum entries)
```

The DisplayServer internally requests a colorspace (likely linear sRGB, on Android HDR10) but the colorspace is implementation dependent. One benefit of this I can imagine (over introducing high/low precision again) is that we won't need another API if we ever make setting the colorspace a public API.

I have been working on the assumption that because it involves changes that would affect a driver which is shared with Windows, this problem could be handled in this PR. author: DarkKilauea

body:
Vulkan is able to submit the colorspace (on some drivers) but unable to report enough of the luminance metadata Wayland expects.

The Wayland API has been built around an expectation that apps will provide correct HDR metadata to the compositor (which is used exclusively by the compositor and not propagated to the monitor). It is implemented in a way that enforces this and any app which does not provide metadata will most likely be forced to SDR regardless of what the vulkan swapchain says (although the behaviour is compositor dependent).

Because most games will not use the wayland API directly even if they do HDR, so within the mesa vulkan drivers (which are open source ones and the only ones the wayland devs have any amount of influence in) there is a path where the vulkan driver itself will use the API to report the colorspace metadata only.

This is “good enough” for games which aren’t wayland native but for the best HDR support we need to submit the luminance values we are using. Even the mesa vulkan driver (when we use the hdr metadata extension) is unable to do this because it doesn’t have the reference luminance metadata, and even then we can look at the implementation and it doesn’t call the correct functions (for what we are trying to do) anyway.

But there is another issue here, the proprietary nvidia drivers do not even make use of the Wayland API to submit a colorspace so to make them work with HDR would require us to use the API directly anyway.
author: ArchercatNEO

body: I see. In that case though, what is the issue with setting the color space using both the Wayland API and Vulkan API? Do they interfere?
author: DarkKilauea

body: Yes, it is a protocol error for both vulkan and the app to use the API simultaneously. It makes sense since allowing otherwise could lead to racy behaviour where the colorspace is set to whoever set it most recently or could even have the vulkan driver always override the app-provided metadata.

Rather than running the editor, I’m exporting the project as a fully packaged .exe file (PCK is embedded). The workflow goes like this:

**On Windows:**

1. [Godot] Enable HDR in project settings (now called “Request HDR Output”)
2. [Godot] Set WorldEnvironment tonemapper to Linear
3. [Godot] Export to Windows using locally compiled Windows export template (ex: “tps-demo.exe”)
4. Open Valve’s [Steam DevKit Management Tool](https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/steamdeck/devkits)
5. Upload the .exe file to Steam Deck OLED via the Management Tool

**On Steam Deck OLED (Gaming Mode):**

1. Go to Library
2. Navigate to Non-Steam
3. Select the Uploaded Game
4. Force Proton Compatibility via Game Properties
5. Press “Play”

This is more or less how developers test their games on Steam Deck. To fully replicate this workflow, you’ll need either a Steam Deck (or Lenovo Legion Go S) or a Linux machine that’s very good at pretending to be a Steam Deck. There’s a good chance you’ll need to use a Deck-clone Linux distribution like Bazzite or HoloISO in order to fully recreate this environment. If recreating a SteamOS-like environment isn’t possible, then it might be enough to have an exported Windows executable + Proton + Gamescope compositor.

body: I have discovered the true issue: there is no problem with HDR in proton or godot, we just default to 0 nits. The image is SDR only because I haven't figured out how to take HDR screenshots yet. What happens is that godot defaults to auto adjusting reference/max luminance which is unavailable under proton. body:
Hi @allenwp,

Sure thing.  While I'm not on the latest rebase of this PR, I went ahead and downloaded your new test project and ran the SDR/HDR stability test. As a control, I first ran it on my Windows 11 OLED Monitor, which is the ASUS PG27AQDM.  

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/44560561-ecf5-4b6f-b482-9574a2e89721

It seems to work as expected, with the only difference being some banding in the dark areas in SDR, which I assume is an expected limitation of the 8-bit color depth of SDR.

As for the Steam Deck OLED, I get this result:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1d7ca20e-d870-4c4e-9c98-801ab0bfaab1

As you can probably see in the video footage, there is a small flicker when the game switches between SDR and HDR. AFAIK, this is intended behavior, and other Steam games also exhibit this behavior when HDR is enabled. Also, it appears that the SDR setting produces an overall brighter image than HDR. This isn't unique to this project, and I've observed a similar behavior when running Microsoft's [D3D12 HDR sample project](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/samples/microsoft/directx-graphics-samples/d3d12-hdr-sample-win32/).

I'm still not sure why this is the case, but I suspect this is going to be a really difficult issue to solve on Deck OLED for a couple of reasons:

**1. Difference between SDR-over-HDR and True SDR**

On Windows, the SDR-HDR stability test is running such that the SDR mode is being emulated inside an HDR container at all times. This is not the case for the Steam Deck OLED (and I suspect OLED TVs as well), where SDR content is running under true SDR mode, and will switch over to HDR mode when the game outputs an HDR signal. 

This would be the equivalent of rapidly switching between HDR on and off in Windows 11. Correct me if I'm mistaken, but I believe it's extremely difficult to align Windows' colors under SDR (i.e. Windows 11 HDR off) to look visually identical (to the human eye) to SDR-over-HDR.

**2. Steam Deck OLED's Brightness Slider**

The Steam Deck OLED uses a relative-value slider to control brightness, and this slider is **shared** between SDR and HDR. In other words, 50% brightness slider in SDR will mean 50% brightness slider in HDR, with no option to have different slider values between the two modes.

In addition, it appears that this brightness slider adjust the overall brightness, even when reference and max luminance are manually set. I could set the project to use a reference luminance of 200 nits and a max luminance of 1,000 nits, but if I set my brightness slider to the lowest setting, the image is getting dimmed no matter what. The exact mechanism isn't completely clear to me yet. It could be a hardware-enforced auto-brightness limiter (ABL) or potential gamma adjustment as [this post says is already used when the slider exceeds 75%](https://www.reddit.com/r/SteamDeck/comments/1lfuxbg/whats_this_change_in_color_mean_when_brightness/).

Assuming we keep the Steam Deck OLED's brightness slider to 75%, which is considered the "calibrated" setting, there could exist a theoretical reference luminance value that is equal between SDR and HDR. I'll keep tinkering with the settings to see if I can find that sweet spot, but Reason 1 could still remain a major thorn.

> @allenwp The reference luminance is 100 nits. It's using the default value that @DarkKilauea placed for the Auto-Adjust HDR brightness in case Auto-Adjust returns 0 nits, as is the case with Proton.

Thanks for confirming this!

**Edit:** The following text is incorrect. I've explained why in [this followup comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3572594626).

This means that the all-important `Window.output_max_linear_value` cannot be calculated, which means that tonemapping, screen glow blending, and any game code that depends on this max value will not function correctly. I’ll look into the Steam Deck developer documentation and reach out to Valve to resolve this issue.

It does make me realize... it might be better to use hardcoded reference and max luminance if *either* reference luminance or maximum luminance cannot be retrieved. Getting one without the other could produce very undesirable results, especially if max luminance is dynamically adjusted, like in the case of [Windows HDR laptops](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3207718463). body:
> This means that the all-important `Window.output_max_linear_value` cannot be calculated, which means that tonemapping, screen glow blending, and any game code that depends on this max value will not function correctly. I’ll look into the Steam Deck developer documentation and reach out to Valve to resolve this issue.
> 
> It does make me realize... it might be better to use hardcoded reference and max luminance if _either_ reference luminance or maximum luminance cannot be retrieved. Getting one without the other could produce very undesirable results, especially if max luminance is dynamically adjusted, like in the case of [Windows HDR laptops](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3207718463). This could result in a very very high max luminance without an appropriately scaled reference luminance that produces a problematically high `output_max_linear_value`.

This is incorrect. The `linear_luminance_scale` in this PR is the 80 nits reference luminance that Windows uses for its buffer. So a max luminance reported as 1015 means that the max Windows buffer value is `1015 / 80 = 12.6875`.

When writing to scene buffers, we use the reference white luminance (can be user defined) and max luminance to calculate `Window.output_max_linear_value`. Let's say reference luminance is 240 nits. This means the max scene value (`Window.output_max_linear_value`) is `1015 / 240 = 4.22917`.

Then in the final steps when writing to the Windows buffer, we transform back to the scale that Windows uses by using the reference multiplier, which in this case is `240 / 80 = 3`. This means the max scene value of `4.22917` is scaled back to its original max buffer value of `12.6875`.

This is why we should expect the max luminance and calculation of `Window.output_max_linear_value` is correctly handled even though we are unable to obtain the reference luminance ("SDR content brightness") from the Windows API, like in the case of Steam Deck. And also why the only outstanding issue is that Godot games on Steam Deck end up looking dark with HDR enabled.

All this to say, I truly appreciate you taking the time to test and confirm that all of this is working well on Steam Deck, iuymatiao! I'll report back when I've heard from Valve about how we should address this issue...

body: When `Window.ouptut_max_linear_value` does not match the display hardware's max value, due to a misconfigured reference/max luminance, glow's screen blend mode will not function well (it will have discontinuity at `ouptut_max_linear_value` when this max value is too low, regardless of the tonemapper) and the tonemap functions will not behave as expected. The solution to these issues would be to simply clip to `ouptut_max_linear_value`, either in tonemap.glsl or blit.glsl. Until now, I have considered this issue to not be a problem worth solving because I believed that some games may be developed with the Linear tonemapper and no glow that uses the screen blend mode. In this specific scenario, it may be desirable to ignore this `ouptut_max_linear_value` and write values above this to the display buffer. ...But recently I've been thinking more about how game developers may use `ouptut_max_linear_value` to produce the brightest colours that a display can reproduce. In this case, even if they're using the Linear tonemapper without glow, they could get very undesirable results when using the `ouptut_max_linear_value`. In fact, `ouptut_max_linear_value` is not trustworthy, as scene values that go above this may not be clipped: Expected | Problem --|-- || In addition to this unexpected problem caused by misconfigured reference/max luminance, I have been struggling to come up with a good design that will allow game developers to simulate what different displays will look like. By adding clipping to blit.glsl, it will become trivial to simulate other displays. All this to say, I am starting to believe that making `Window.ouptut_max_linear_value` absolutely trustworthy is of utmost importance to make for a simple, easy, and intuitive SDR/HDR/EDR development experience. I am struggling to see substantial downsides to performing clipping in blit.glsl and I see a number additional benefits: glow blending and tonemapping will always work well and making editor functions to simulate other displays becomes trivial. **Update:** I've been playing around with clipping before writing to the display buffer today. This has a consequence I hadn't thought about: extremely bright colours remain more stable between SDR and HDR when using the Linear tonemapper. I see this as a positive that gives more control to the author by unifying colours between SDR and HDR. The reason this difference happens is because unclipped colours will be tonemapped and/or clipped by the display in its native colour space, while pre-clipped colours can be correctly represented by the display without further modification by the display.
author: allenwp

body:
> After running a couple more tests on Steam Deck OLED, my guess is that, at 75% brightness slider, an HDR game would need a reference luminance of ~350 nits to get similar colors as SDR Mode.

I heard back from Valve and confirmed this is about right: reference white luminance for SDR is set at 400 nits.

Also, as demonstrated by iuymatiao, max luminance that is reported by Steam Deck doesn't change as brightness is decreased. From my brief discussion with Valve, the suggested reference white luminance for HDR games on Steam Deck is actually around 200 to 300 nits so that more HDR headroom is available (users can crank the brightness up quite high to compensate for a darker game if they want). This is different than how Windows, Mac OS, iOS, and Android handle things. It appears that Steam Deck's HDR implementation is built around trying to work with decisions made by early HDR games on Windows that didn't make use of Window's SDR Content Brightness.

Additionally, Windows defaults to 240 nits for its "SDR Content Brightness" (which is what we use for our HDR reference white luminance when this value is available from the OS).

All that to say, I'm leaning towards defaulting to a 200 nits reference white luminance on all platforms for the [reasons stated here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#pullrequestreview-2659049328). Because Steam Deck was designed to make existing Windows HDR games that ignore SDR Content Brightness look good, it makes sense to match the default reference white luminance use by other HDR Windows games, like Ratchet and Clank: A Rift Apart. This 200 nits default is effectively the same as what [BT.2408](https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REP-BT.2408) recommends, is close to the Windows default of 240, and is on the low end of what Valve suggests for Steam Deck in our case.

author: iuymatiao

body:
> Am I correct to assume that this 200 nits default for reference luminance is still separate from the Windows 11 SDR Content Brightness (or other platform equivalent settings)

Yes, it is simply the fallback value that is used when retrieving SDR Content Brightness fails. In practice, this means it will only ever be used on Steam Deck Windows emulation or equivalent.

> Am I correct in assuming that this 200 nits reference luminance, when combined with the display’s max luminance, is used to compute the initial color rendering pass before being “tonemapped” to match the user’s OS-level preferences (ex: 115 nits)?

On Steam Deck with a Windows game, this would mean this mapping from Godot post-tonemapping values (or Godot scene values with Linear tonemapper) to Steam Deck pre-system-brightness nits:

Godot post-tonemap value | Steam Deck OLED nits (pre-system brightness) | Steam Deck OLED physical nits
--|--|--
1.0 | 200 nits | Depends on Steam Deck brightness setting
5.075 (`output_max_linear_value`) | 1015 nits | Depends on Steam Deck brightness setting

And, of course, you can still manually set the reference luminance from in-game settings, as you can do with my test project. If a player sets the reference luminance to 115 nits instead, you would get these values:

Godot post-tonemap value | Steam Deck OLED nits (pre-system brightness) | Steam Deck OLED physical nits
--|--|--
1.0 | 115 nits | Depends on Steam Deck brightness setting
8.83 (`output_max_linear_value`) | 1015 nits | Depends on Steam Deck brightness setting

body:
I guess my question is more on why the 200 nits default value is so important if the user is allowed to adjust their reference luminance up and down.

Assuming the current behavior of this PR where Godot will return a default reference luminance value of 100 nits (because Proton doesn’t return a proper luminance value when set to auto-adjust), how does color rendering break down in this scenario? I assume that `output_max_linear_value` can still be calculated as `1015 / 100 = 10.15`, with a still usable reference multiplier of `100 / 80 = 1.2` when writing to the Windows buffer.

Or is this a case where the lack of a reliable “auto-adjust” implementation from the Steam Deck OLED means that 100 nits on Deck OLED cannot be assumed to look identical to 100 nits on Windows 11 (using SDR Content Brightness)?

My apologies if it sounds like I’m overly probing into this topic. I’m just trying to understand the important of these default values given the importance of getting this right being implied in [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3572594626).
author: iuymatiao

body:
> I guess my question is more on why the 200 nits default value is so important if the user is allowed to adjust their reference luminance up and down.

Implementing in-game settings to adjust reference luminance is optional; some (likely many) will ship without these in-game settings, so there will be no way for the player to adjust reference luminance.

> Assuming the current behavior of this PR where Godot will return a default reference luminance value of 100 nits (because Proton doesn’t return a proper luminance value when set to auto-adjust), how does color rendering break down in this scenario? I assume that `output_max_linear_value` can still be calculated as `1015 / 100 = 10.15`, with a still usable reference multiplier of `100 / 80 = 1.2` when writing to the Windows buffer.

Color rendering does not break down, regardless of whether this default fallback reference luminance is set to 100, 200, 400, 80, or any other number. I made a mistake when I originally wrote [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3567997089). I apologize for the confusion.

> Or is this a case where the lack of a reliable “auto-adjust” implementation from the Steam Deck OLED means that 100 nits on Deck OLED cannot be assumed to look identical to 100 nits on Windows 11 (using SDR Content Brightness)?

Having HDR match SDR apparent brightness is no longer a goal for Steam Deck because when the system brightness of the Steam Deck is turned down, there is no increase in available HDR headroom. Steam Deck behaves differently than all other platforms in this way: with other platforms, additional HDR headroom becomes available as the user turns down the system brightness, so matching SDR brightness is the best way to give a good user/player experience and also maximize the available HDR headroom. This is simply not possible on Steam Deck.

> My apologies if it sounds like I’m overly probing into this topic. I’m just trying to understand the important of these default values given the importance of getting this right being implied in [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3572594626).

No problem, I'm happy to explain!

But to answer your primary question about why the fallback default reference luminance is important: This fallback default will determine two things when a game does not provide in-game settings to adjust Godot's reference luminance:

1) How bright or dark HDR games appear to players, especially in relation to other HDR games, SDR games, and the Steam Deck OS UI.
2) How much HDR headroom will be available.

These two things are in tension with each other: In order to best serve point number 2, we could set the reference luminance at 10 nits and this would give players the most HDR headroom. But this would make games appear far too dark, going against point 1.

From my understanding of how the system brightness setting was engineered, it appears that it was designed to make existing Windows HDR games that did not make use of Windows SDR Content Brightness look good. I believe (based on a small sample size) that most existing Windows HDR games that did not make use of Windows SDR Content Brightness probably used a reference white luminance of around 200 nits. This would make sense given [BT.2408](https://www.itu.int/pub/R-REP-BT.2408) (203 nits) and the default SDR Content Brightness of Windows (240 nits). The 100 nits reference luminance standard comes from cinema/home cinema standards that expect a darker viewing environment, so I suspect few games are authored with this reference white luminance.

And finally, after talking with someone at Valve who worked on HDR for Steam Deck, they said around 200-300 nits is probably what we want to target.

So all of this leads me to think that around 200 nits is probably the best balance between point 1 and 2. I suspect that players would often find that games with a 100 nits reference luminance appear "too dark". Although this is subjective, it really comes down to expectations based on other games that they play on their Steam Deck, which may be HDR or SDR.

I'm going to put together a demo project and try things out myself before pushing the change to the default; I found someone in the game dev community of my city who's willing to let me try out their Steam Deck OLED so I can see for myself and sanity-check the assumptions I've been making.

Hopefully that clears things up!
author: allenwp

body:
> So all of this leads me to think that around 200 nits is probably the best balance between point 1 and 2. I suspect that players would often find that games with a 100 nits reference luminance appear "too dark". Although this is subjective, it really comes down to expectations based on other games that they play on their Steam Deck, which may be HDR or SDR.

I empirically find 200 nits to be a good default, mostly because it's what the vast majority OLED of TVs/monitors can consistently show in a 100% window without ABL kicking in. In comparison, a higher value like 240 nits isn't a given. As of late 2025, the very best OLED monitors can do roughly 300 nits in a 100% window.

Darker values like 120 nits (sRGB standard) make more sense in a dark room environment, but they will show their limits in brighter office enviroments, or even in a dark room when playing games that have bright elements (the HUD will look too dark relative to the game).

body:
### Latest rebase

This mostly looked good! Thanks for doing this!! I've pushed a commit to fix up a couple of things so that my big overhaul to tonemapping and AgX with HDR is now complete. I did another trivial rebase while I was at it, since I needed for force push anyway.

### Comments and minor changes

I've added a number of comments to document our rationale; normally a developer would be able to look at the PR to determine this, but there's no way anyone in the future will be searching through the hundreds of comments of this PR to find this information, so it's important for these notes to be presented in code comments.

I've fully removed the `float hdr_linear_luminance_scale` variable from D3D12 and Metal because these drivers have strictly defined values. It makes sense to keep this variable for Vulkan for its use in the Android PR, for example.

### Clipping

I've added clipping to `output_max_linear_value` because of the rationale I described in [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#issuecomment-3593110507). This may have a noticeable impact on the appearance of bright colours when using the Linear tonemapper with some displays compared to the previous state of this PR and I really do think this is a good thing. This clipping is very helpful in producing consistent colours between SDR and HDR mode. If you're used to the existing behaviour of this PR, it might take some getting used to, but I think this new behaivour will be ideal for any developers who are creating a game that runs in both SDR and HDR mode.

### Docs changes

I've done a second pass on the docs for `Window.get_output_max_linear_value()`. In this revision, I've modified the sample code to be more flexible for colours that do not have a component that equals `1.0` by introducing a `normalize_color` function. I've been using this normalize function in my test project and find it's the most convenient way to use `get_output_max_linear_value()`. I also added notes that this approach can only be used when using no tonemaping or the Linear tonemapper.

``` GDScript
func _process(_delta: float):
	# output_max_linear_value may change often, so do this every frame.
	# max_linear_value is only valid when using no tonemapping or the
	# Linear tonemapper.
	var max_linear_value = get_window().get_output_max_linear_value()
	# Replace this with your color:
	var original_color = Color.PURPLE
	# Normalize to max_linear_value to produce the brightest color possible,
	# regardless of SDR or HDR output:
	var bright_color = normalize_color(original_color, max_linear_value)


func normalize_color(srgb_color, max_linear_value = 1.0):
	# Color must be linear-encoded to use math operations.
	var linear_color = srgb_color.srgb_to_linear()
	var max_rgb_value = maxf(linear_color.r, maxf(linear_color.g, linear_color.b))
	var brightness_scale = max_linear_value / max_rgb_value
	linear_color *= brightness_scale
	# Undo changes to the alpha channel, which should not be modified.
	linear_color.a = srgb_color.a
	# Convert back to nonlinear sRGB encoding, which is required for Color in
	# Godot unless stated otherwise.
	return linear_color.linear_to_srgb()
```

### Editor changes

I noticed the `ColorPicker` needs to be enhanced to work with HDR output in addition to the other editor previews.

I believe the "Enable HDR for editor previews when HDR output is enabled" commit should be separated into its own followup PR (similar to the Android HDR PR) in order to improve the review process: This way, members who are experts in reviewing editor changes will be able to focus on editor changes, rather than needing to wade through the vast number of changes of this PR that are not related to the editor. Besides that commit, this PR has almost zero changes to the editor, and I think this is a good thing for the review process.

This "[HDR output] editor enhancements" PR that adds all of the non-critical editor changes can be used to track other things that come up, like the `ColorPicker`.

As another benefit, it means we can keep this PR in a "ready to merge" state so we can get it into 4.7 dev 1 without risk of editor enhancements blocking it :)

### Squashing

As always, go ahead and squash my commits when you've reviewed them; I simply left them separate for it to be easier to see what I've changed.

While testing, I was connecting and disconnecting monitors a fair bit and got into a situation where Godot reported this error:
```
ERROR: platform\windows\display_server_windows.cpp:1646 - Failed to get SDR white level for screen: 1, adapterId: 0x000000000000CDAA, id: 4352
```
And then stopped responding entirely to changes in `SDRWhiteLevel`, regardless of whether I turned "request HDR output" on or off or moved the window between displays. I took a look at the code and noticed that it was written such that it would stop attempting to read changes in `SDRWhiteLevel` after the first failed attempt, as [suggested](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#discussion_r2566234742) by @bruvzg.

I've committed and squashed a change to only stop reporting error messages instead of permanently giving up on reading `SDRWhiteLevel` for the display. This should resolve the issue that I had, but is different than the logic that @bruvzg suggested. Feel free to clean it up further, but the previous suggestion to block future attempts to read `SDRWhiteLevel` is not functional, it seems.

I've also renamed my old test project to be a ["Godot HDR output porting test project "](https://github.com/allenwp/godot-hdr-output-test-project). This older test project is designed solely for implementing the HDR output feature on new platforms. The official [HDR output demo project](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-demo-projects/pull/1287) supersedes it for general demonstration purposes.

Finally, I've created trackers for HDR output-related [proposals](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/13750) and [issues & PRs](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/113959). From the description:

body:
I updated my [bug report comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#pullrequestreview-3746182902) with my system info.

After some more trying, the bug doesn't happen 100% of the time for me. But thankfully, it still happens most of the time so I was able to catch when debugging. It seems that sometimes when the `WM_DISPLAYCHANGE` event fires, the `DXGI_OUTPUT_DESC1` is still reporting `DXGI_COLOR_SPACE_RGB_FULL_G22_NONE_P709`. I suspect that the pre-optimized code worked because it would poll `DXGI_OUTPUT_DESC1` every frame and pick up the delayed change to `DXGI_COLOR_SPACE_RGB_FULL_G2084_NONE_P2020`, thus correctly updating the Window to show that HDR output is now supported.

From looking at this new code it seems that there is probably another bug that exists: As I shared in a [previous comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94496#discussion_r2737643003), changes to maximum luminance do not trigger the `WM_DISPLAYCHANGE` event, which means that maximum luminance must be polled, just the same as `SDRWhiteLevel`. This is because any time the screen brightness on a laptop with a built-in HDR screen is changed, the maximum luminance values will change, so this will happen often on some screens.
