body:
@allenwp I believe I've resolved the issues you discovered. 
@blueskythlikesclouds FYI so you can look at the performance numbers.

I've reverted back to loading the entire HDR state on each frame. This does undo some of the performance improvements gained, but should guarantee HDR output matches the screen in all situations. *insert gripe about Windows missing events for HDR display changes*

I tried a number of approaches to reduce the performance overhead:

1. Calling DXGI and gathering reference luminance in another thread. This didn't end up working due to the COM model DXGI uses, which expects to be called from the same thread once initialized.
2. Batching all calls needed to gather information for all displays into a smaller set, reducing the number of round trips through the kernel as much as possible. This actually ended up slower than what I eventually landed on due to allocation overhead and processing display paths that were not actually needed. This approach may be faster if there are many HDR windows on many displays, but it is slower for the common case of one window on one display. You can see that approach here: https://github.com/DarkKilauea/godot/tree/rendering/hdr-output-cache
3. Keeping the original approach but reducing the number of trips through the kernel as much as possible. This is what I merged into this PR.

My latest performance numbers are:

Metric  | HDR Disabled (usec) | HDR Requested Batching (usec) | HDR Requested Previous (usec) | HDR Requested Latest (usec)
-- | -- | -- | -- | --
Average | 0.984962406 | 348.518797 | 213.4706767 | 200.3278195
95th Percentile | 2 | 717.6 | 475.6 | 434.8
99th Percentile | 3 | 844.16 | 532.08 | 479.72

> On Windows 10, when independent flip is engaged (according to PresentMon), I seem to be able to get 2 frames latency with v-sync on, less than 2 ms latency with v-sync off. (No variable refresh rate.)

This checks out with triple buffering being used. If you were able to [opt into using double buffering](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4065) instead, you could get a single frame of latency at the cost of less stable framerates when the framerate drops below the monitor refresh rate.

The NVIDIA Control Panel has a setting to control whether triple buffering is used in OpenGL applications.
author: Calinou

body:
> > On Windows 10, when independent flip is engaged (according to PresentMon), I seem to be able to get 2 frames latency with v-sync on, less than 2 ms latency with v-sync off. (No variable refresh rate.)
> 
> This checks out with triple buffering being used. If you were able to [opt into using double buffering](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4065) instead, you could get a single frame of latency at the cost of less stable framerates when the framerate drops below the monitor refresh rate.

Turns out the reason for 2 frames is stupid: I forgot to wait for the frame latency waitable object before rendering the first frame. Fixing that gives 1 frame of latency (actually less than 1).

The number of frames in the present queue is controlled by `IDXGISwapChain2::SetMaximumFrameLatency`, currently set to 1, which is double buffering (if the code had waited properly.) For actual triple buffering it should be set to 2.


> Tested locally, I get a crash on startup with the message `Segmentation fault` when the project manager starts (the crash handler doesn't run). The window is created, but it only ever renders black before crashing a second later.

So, it was also crashing the NVIDIA driver on my Optimus setup. I am not sure if it is the same crash that you have, but from what I have managed to gather this is a use-after-free inside NVIDIA's driver inside the `wglDXRegisterObjectNV` call after resizing the swap chain, so the crash can only happen after resizing the window, (which the Project Manager does once during startup).

I just tried to reorder some calls. Maybe that's all it needed to fix the crash?

body:
My idea on how to use the frame latency waitable:

- Wait inside `DisplayServerWindows::process_events` before processing input.
    - Supposedly Godot can run CPU-bound processing before the waitable is signalled, but I don't know any processing in Godot that does not depend on handling user input.
- If the current focused window has v-sync enabled, we wait for this window to present.
- If the current focused window have v-sync disabled:
    - If there are other windows with v-sync enabled, wait for any one of these to present (wait until the earliest one has presented).
    - If none of the other windows have v-sync enabled, don't wait at all.

body:
So I tested out this PR and it appears to be functional for the most part. PresentMon reports "Hardware Composed: Independent Flip". It definitely needs a bit of cleanup though, so I'll see if I can salvage this work. Some things I noticed:

- Currently the max FPS seems to be dramatically affected. When running the [latency tester](https://github.com/KeyboardDanni/godot-latency-tester) with V-Sync disabled, `master` maxes out at 1846 FPS, while this PR only manages 660 FPS.
  - CPU/swapchain wait should be removed or made optional, and frametimes measured to judge impact.
- We need to make sure it's compatible with window alpha channel.
  - `CreateSwapChainForHwnd` should be replaced with `CreateSwapChainForComposition` for direct composition as in #99387.
- Double-buffer/triple-buffer option is not exposed to projects like it is for RenderingDevice. That is, currently it's hardcoded to use `SetMaximumFrameLatency(2)`. The code can be changed to `SetMaximumFrameLatency(1)` and this successfully lowers input latency down to just 1 frame (which is about as perfect as you can get), but this really should be a ProjectSetting.
- V-Sync setting logic is incomplete.
  - Initialization code ignores the game's requested V-Sync mode and always sets Adaptive if available.
- Screen Y-flip logic should be consolidated. It's unclear to me how much of this is boilerplate that needs to be removed.
- Various other `TODO`s in the code.

Edit: Also there's possibly some unnecessary registering/unregistering of objects and framebuffer clearing happening.
author: KeyboardDanni

body:
Something seems to be wrong with how the GL/DX interop handles locking resources, and I'm not sure if the problem is with the interop strategy here, threading, nVidia's drivers, or the `NV_DX_interop` extension itself.

Basically I'm not happy that the default strategy (drawing directly to the shared buffer) drops the max FPS of a basic project from 1800 FPS to 600. The intermediate buffer approach runs better at 1200 FPS, and I tested performance with the TPS demo and found the in-game FPS only dropped by about 5%. That would have been good enough for me, except I noticed some pretty serious desktop responsiveness issues with V-Sync disabled. Things like the volume OSD, mousing over controls in other applications, watching video on another display... all choppy, delayed, and inconsistent and just not a good experience. I didn't notice these issues with OpenGL native presentation or the D3D12 renderer.

After some experimentation, it seems the main culprit is `wglDXLockObjectsNV` and `wglDXUnlockObjectsNV`, at least from the surface. If I don't unlock/lock the GLDX interop object(s) during `present()`, I don't seem to have the responsiveness issues, and max FPS goes all the way up to 2000. But also this is a *bad idea*, because [the extension's specification](https://registry.khronos.org/OpenGL/extensions/NV/WGL_NV_DX_interop.txt) says you **must** lock interop objects when accessed from GL, and you **must** unlock them before accessing them from DX, or behavior is undefined.

Maybe there's some other way to limit the overhead of the locking mechanism. Maybe there's a resource contention or threading issue which can be avoided on our end somehow. Unfortunately, my attempts to debug this have not been successful yet, as the problem seems to go away if I run the program through Nsight Systems (in fact, doing this seems to both remove the stall and break V-Sync).

body:
> Rather than copying and modifying a `DisplayServer`, could it make sense to make a `DisplayServer` that wraps another `DisplayServer`?

This would require modifications to all of the platform-specific DisplayServer classes, which I wanted to avoid.

For example, in `DisplayServerWindows`'s constructor, it calls its private `_create_window` method, which creates an on-screen surface, so these functions would need to be modified to call some virtual method to set up the screen and surface.

But, yes, that would probably be a better long-term solution. If I can find the time, I'll do some research into the exact changes that would be needed.

> > Users should use the old workflow which is to have a child MeshInstance3D with `SHADOW_CASTING_SETTING_SHADOWS_ONLY` and have the source mesh use SHADOW_CASTING_SETTING_OFF. Doing so has no additional cost over using shadow_mesh, but gives the user full control over how the shadow is drawn.
> 
> Performance gains can be significant with 4-split PSSM (or in scenes with lots of point lights with shadows enabled) if you have lots of complex meshes.

Using nearby LODs won't be as bad as a completely different mesh for shadows (like in the OP issue). I think https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/2600 would be better off with an LOD bias for shadows specifically. Remember, when used in the depth prepass, using a different mesh (even a different LOD of the same mesh) will totally break rendering. However, using a lower LOD for _shadows only_ maybe be feasible.

Looks like the vector 'grows exponentially' so it would have to be exactly sized to hit near a power of 2 to hit this dereference check and possibly cause a crash

Edit:
Unfortunately all powers of 2 are not multiples of 12...
e.g.

``` 
for LocalVector<Vector3>:

42 x 12 = 504b (42 x sizeof(Vector3))
getptr(size -1) == byte 500 (last float* address is the last 4 bytes of the buffer)
resize(42) will set capacity to 512 (next larger power of 2)
500 + 16 = 516 (4 bytes past the end of the 512 byte/2^9byte capacity)
```

> It looks like we should use `reserve()` instead of `resize()` here.. Also, upon further inspection I suspect this buffer may cause [this error](https://github.com/RenderKit/embree/blob/5730b150471602d6dc02d9b7d8a4a6ce9ceffe16/kernels/common/scene_points.cpp#L47C1-L48C83): `throw_RTCError(RTC_ERROR_INVALID_OPERATION, "data must be 4 bytes aligned");` on 32 bit systems that don't align their malloc to 16 bytes!!!
> 
> Even worse: this would only fail on release builds since debug builds automatically add padding to align to `sizeof(uint64_t)`

After a [more careful reading](https://github.com/RenderKit/embree/tree/5730b150471602d6dc02d9b7d8a4a6ce9ceffe16?tab=readme-ov-file#description-description-92) I realize the byte alignment requirement for the _start_ of the buffer is [4 bytes](https://github.com/RenderKit/embree/blob/5730b150471602d6dc02d9b7d8a4a6ce9ceffe16/kernels/common/scene_triangle_mesh.cpp#L37) (not 16).

x86_32 malloc implementations seem to align to 8 bytes so I can stop worrying :D

on 32 bit GNU/Linux for example, where realloc/malloc specification says

>The address of a block returned by malloc or realloc in GNU systems is always a multiple of eight (or sixteen on 64-bit systems).

or msvcrt for 32 bit windows

>In Visual C++, the fundamental alignment is the alignment that's required for a double, or 8 bytes. In code that targets 64-bit platforms, it's 16 bytes.

body:
Just passing by. A few thoughts:
- `T const &` is inconsistent with the rest of codebase. `const T &` is preferred.
- There is string appening functionality, `StringBuilder`. I'm not sure how to use it for the late sign insertion, but there's likely a clever way to solve that.
- `String str = "("` deserves the optimization, too.


> There's quite a lot of examples of `thread_local LocalVector` used for similar purposes, so I wonder about introducing a `LocalString` class, which would use `LocalVector` inside of it. Not sure if it would be worth it if there's not many uses for it though

The `thread_local` thing is being done with `LocalVector` because it features a capacity feature, which `Vector` doesn't. In addition, `LocalVector` doesn't have a thread-safe refcount, which makes it more performant and the right option when you know you don't need such a thing. My point is that `thread_local Vector` and `thread_local String` would be possible if `Vector` featured the aforementioned capacity-reserve feature. Adding it would avoid having to emulate it in certain parts of the engine where the `Vector` is sized to what it would be the capacity and the size is managed externally.

In other words, at some point my view is that it would be ideal that `Vector` and `LocalVector` were just two specializations of the same template, with better names. So, `Vector` would be `LocalVector` plus copy-on-write
I opened a proposal time ago about this: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/5144.

We could even have a copy-on-write specialization which is not thread-safe, which may be a better fit for strings. I'd say that all of this would need to be discussed carefully because there are things yelling to be improved, such as these vector types getting more telling names and finding out the most precise set of features each needs across the codebase.

body:
My understanding of the current implementation of the classes related to `EditorResourcePreview` makes it seem like [`_handles`] cannot be meaningfully used for filtering custom resource types. It invokes [`get_class`] and passes the result to [`_handles`]. 

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/93d270693079ea7802c9e1334a2e0ecd8529eeed/editor/editor_resource_preview.cpp#L174-L178 https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/93d270693079ea7802c9e1334a2e0ecd8529eeed/editor/editor_resource_preview.cpp#L197

According to the documentation [`get_class`] ignores `class_name` defintions (which similarly applies to the name of C# classes). Given [`get_class`] is not a virtual method, it cannot be overridden. As such the `type` parameter is usually a built-in type. 
> Note: This method ignores `class_name` declarations. If this object's script has defined a class_name, the base, built-in class name is returned instead.

(The alternative path is ultimately based on what [`ResourceFormatLoader`] listst as the type, which similarly uses a built-in)

However, this does not prevent us from creating custom preview images. Simply returning `true` from [`_handles`] makes it so the preview generator in question is up for consideration. (Though one _might_ want to narrow the selection a bit by comparing it to the inherited type)

The actual filtering can then be done in [`_generate`], which gets a reference to the `Resource` for which we want to generate a preview. Returning `Texture2D.new()` indicates that this generator actually couldn't handle the resource, so another one will be tried next.

```gdscript
class_name CustomResource
extends Resource
```

```gdscript
@tool
extends EditorResourcePreviewGenerator

func _handles(type: String) -> bool:
  return type == "Resource" # Without technical limitations this would be "CustomResource" (in this example).

func _generate(resource: Resource, size: Vector2i, metadata: Dictionary) -> Texture2D:
  if resource is not CustomResource: return Texture2D.new();
  
  var image := Image.create(size.x, size.y, true, Image.FORMAT_RGBA8)
  # Draw stuf…

  return ImageTexture.from(image);
```
Then add/remove it in the relevant place (generally `_enter_tree`/`_exit_tree` of a plugin).
```gdscript
EditorInterface.get_resource_previewer().add_preview_generator(generator)
EditorInterface.get_resource_previewer().remove_preview_generator(generator)  
``` 

[`_handles`]: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_editorresourcepreviewgenerator.html#class-editorresourcepreviewgenerator-private-method-generate-small-preview-automatically
[`_generate`]: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_editorresourcepreviewgenerator.html#class-editorresourcepreviewgenerator-private-method-generate
[`get_class`]: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_object.html#class-object-method-get-class
[`ResourceFormatLoader`]: https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/classes/class_resourceformatloader.html#class-resourceformatloader-private-method-handles-type

body:
So I tested this and it works, but the API is super weird.
`add_context_menu_item()` does not add an item, it defines an item that will appear when plugin is activated. This means that each plugin can add only one menu item. The function's first argument is an icon, which is completely optional for menus. Also if you don't call this method, the editor will crash.
There is `SUBMENU_SLOT_NONE` which does nothing (?) and `SUBMENU_SLOT_FILESYSTEM_CREATE`, which is a part of different enum and can't be used.

I think instead of `_can_handle()`, there could be `_popup_menu(arguments: Array)` virtual function. Though maybe `paths` is fine, not sure where else we will want to add options.
Inside that function the user is supposed to call `add_context_menu_item()`, as many times as they want. I'd change the signature to `add_context_menu_item(text: String, callback: Callable, icon: Texture2D = null, shortcut: Shortcut = null)`. The plugin would have a vector of structs representing added menu items. The editor would then use this vector to add menu items to the PopupMenu.

Instead of keeping an array of plugins per slot, I think it can be a single LocalVector. When opening menu, go through the vector and check the plugin slot. If the slot matches, call `_popup_menu()` and then add options to menu.

To make your life easier, this can be handled with internal methods:
`add_options_from_plugins(PopupMenu *p_menu, ContextMenuSlot p_slot, const PackedStringArray &p_paths)` (this can be a method in EditorData; you need to keep the registered plugins somewhere)
`EditorContextMenuPlugin::add_options(const PackedStringArray &p_paths)` - it would clear the option structs vector, call the virtual `_popup_menu()` and then add items based on added options.

Feel free to ask if something is not clear. You can also join [the developer chat](https://chat.godotengine.org/).

body:
Based on the recommendations, the final API has been adjusted; ```_can_handle``` has been changed to ```_popup_menu```. The method ```add_context_menu_item ```will store data in a local HashMap, meaning that menu items with the same name will be unique. Additionally, to enhance understanding, submenu slots are now on the same level as other slots. Below is the example code.

```gdscript
extends EditorContextMenuPlugin
const PLUG = preload("res://addons/csv-update/plug.svg")

func _popup_menu(paths: PackedStringArray) -> bool:
	## The return result will determine whether to display the added options.
	add_context_menu_item("File Custom options", handle, PLUG)
	return true

func handle(paths):
	print("file context item handle:", paths)

```

Unless I have an incomplete understanding of what exports are for, this wasn't supposed to be a supported use case for .NET. That's what I gathered from reading [this issue](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/89860), which suggests that the problem is the presence of the non-tool type itself and not so much whether it's actually used in the tool context.

The only solution I can think of without simply forbidding these kinds of exports is to get the SDK to wholly discard the implementation of the non-tool script and provide one without any methods, constructors or static initializers, so non-tool code can't run but a correct type can be given.

I think it should still be possible to simply not use the `[Export]` attribute, and still allow regular public members of the non-tool type so non-tool code can interact with it.

When the point list is seperated into $r1$ and $r2$, the middle point( $p_m$ ) is placed in both list: $r1 = \[p_0,...,p_m\]$ and $r2 = \[p_m,...,p_k\]$. When the two list are reattached the middle point is is kept, with the extra middle point removed: $resultList = r1 \cup r2 = \[p_0,...,p_m,...,p_k\]$.

Self intersection errors start becoming a problem when you have a complex  shape and a high optimization value.

body:
I checked it works on the MRP in the issue by moving both cameras away and finding that the sound comes back when either of them is moved back towards the sound source.  

Most of this PR improves comment grammar and renames some variables.  The main change is to loop through the cameras, pick the one with highest attenuation value (usually the closest), and then run `AudioStreamPlayer3D::_calc_output_vol()` for its direction and distance.

The current implementation in the Master branch loops through all the cameras, calculates `output_volume_vector` values for each active one (over-writing earlier calculations in the loop), before returning this array from the `AudioStreamPlayer3D::_update_panning()` function.  This means that only the final camera in the list is considered.

This PR code is quite out-dated and does not include the change in the calculation of this array where it uses `AudioStreamPlayer3D::_calc_output_vol_stereo()` for the stereo case.

Knowing about this, I can predict the following case:  

Two audio listeners on either side of the source, on the left and on the right, about the same distance.  As each one moves closer or further, the one that is closer changes side, so you will get all the sound coming through the left speaker and then popping to all come out of the right speaker.

Perhaps we should calculate this `output_volume_vector` for each camera and select the maximum value in each mono channel individually, left or right, so that if the listeners are on either side of the source the sound comes to both ears and not just one.

Also discuss why computing the max value is better than computing the average value for the volume from the cameras.

IMO it would be best if the audio samples could be fully computed for each camera and then be mixed together. However, currently this seems not to be possible because the Doppler effect is simulated using the pitch scale of the playbacks of the audio stream (so it is not associated with the cameras).

What you suggest sounds like a big refactor of how AudioStreamPlayers interact with cameras and viewports, so I think this is out of scope of this PR (and my PR https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/114080). I would rather prefer a fix that easily improves the current situation and enables sound for split screen mode and put the more sophisticated solution into the backlog

This maybe isn't the most minimal of MRPs, but it does reproduce the crash/regression mentioned above: [cached-parser-crash.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/16364702/cached-parser-crash.zip)

It's essentially just a clean project with the [Cheatsheet](https://godotengine.org/asset-library/asset/1747) add-on added to it, but with one tiny modification done to it, which is that `scripts/cheatsheet.gd` now references `scripts/argument.gd`, specifically in its `register` function (although the location doesn't seem to matter):

```diff
func register(name: String, callback: Callable) -> Command:
	var command := db.register(name, callback)
+	if not command.args.is_empty():
+		print(command.args[0].name)
	commands_changed.emit()
	return command
```

That modification causes the crash, and without that modification the project loads just fine.

EDIT: There's a more minimal MRP here as well: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94697#issuecomment-2248442900

Unlike what mentioned in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/86234#issuecomment-1859117533 , I decided always set the no delay option.

That was the original intent, and is in line with most implementations:

https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=542401

https://issues.chromium.org/issues/41152920

https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=102079

It's worth noting that languages like go, defaults to disable the Nagle's algorithm even if most OSes would otherwise have different default ([see here](https://pkg.go.dev/net#TCPConn.SetNoDelay)).

We should evaluate if we want to do something similar in Godot's socket implementation (in its own proposal/PR).

Already expressed my opinion on this in one short emote, but...

The additional note about this behavior is frankly way too oversized and will result in much fewer readers spending time to read about this niche scenario. Its presence in multiple descriptions does not help, as the otherwise simple concepts are seemingly bloated with the same piece of information all over the page. It makes it difficult to maintain them, as well.

The behavior and an explanation in detail should be documented somewhere else. A recommendation not to use delta for time sensitive stuff may still exist. Most people do not need to know why, only what to do about it.
author: Mickeon

body:
I tend to agree that it's a bit verbose, especially when repeated in so many locations.

I'm also slightly worried about our tendency to put such big notes in many locations, which each need to be translated individually by translators (where each description is one msgid), with the risk of using different language in each if they're not aware that it's a repeat of an already translated part of description.

That being said, I understand the need to provide more advanced information on some edge cases. I'm not sure what's the best way to do that.

A pattern we'd use sometimes is to put the detailed docs in one place, and only include a short blurb in other locations with a backreference to the detailed one.

body:
> In my case, before I knew about this stuff, while running on default settings with Max FPS set to 1, I expected process delta to be 1, but it is smaller than expected (0.133).

This is why delta is `~0.13` in this situation, assuming the **Physics FPS** and **Max Physics Steps per Frame** project settings are set to their respective defaults (`60` and `8`):

```
physics_fps/max_physics_steps_per_frame
60/8.0
= 7.5

1/slowdown_factor
1/7.5
= 0.13333333333333333333
```

Being able to adjust snap to pixel on a per-CanvasItem basis sounds like a good idea. I've noticed that some use cases can benefit from having this enabled on specific 2D nodes only.

That said, I would particularly appreciate this for Control snapping (which uses a different system where snapping is enabled by default). Snapping controls to pixels is generally undesired for controls that follow a camera projection (e.g. in the [3D Waypoints](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-demo-projects/tree/master/3d/waypoints) demo), as it'll cause the controls to visibly snap to pixels when at a resolution higher than the default in the `canvas_items` stretch mode.

That said, it could also be argued that **Snap Controls to Pixels** should obey `canvas_items` scaling and adjust the snapping distance accordingly. The visible snapping on high-resolution displays doesn't look great for animation either.

In general, this makes me wonder if setting this to **Disabled** should forcibly disable control snapping to pixels in projects that have **Snap Controls to Pixels** enabled (the default).

body:
Before:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ba187676-0794-4dff-87b3-80e952441347)


After:

![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/931b012f-7be8-4c29-b859-774d1550d14b)

Notes:

The mesh on the left is from #67891; the mesh on the right is the same GLB file with explicitly generated tangents via gltf-transform. This PR relies on *correctly* generated tangents: when UVs are mirrored, the vertices on the mirror seam need to be duplicated and have two tangents, one pointing one way and the other pointing the other way (with TBN winding flipped between the two).

The reason I mention this is that the way Godot generates new tangents is actually incorrect: it does this using the current geometry indexing, instead of doing unindex/reindex. This prevents tangent generation from creating new vertices. This was changed ~6 years ago to make morph targets work, and since nobody noticed in 6 years it's probably fine (?), but this happens to work properly because the model in question has the seam in the index data in GLB whether or not tangents are generated, so things work out "magically". If you instead optimize the basketball GLB, welding the vertices in the file itself, then this PR does not fix the UV mapping issue because tangent generation is incapable of "unwelding" the vertices back.

So in that respect this is a partial fix, since the model needs to either carry tangent data or not result in incorrect tangents generated during import; otherwise the LODs may still result in significant texture distortion along the mirror seams. But it does fully fix the referenced issue.

body:
Please give more detailed info on what's the issue this PR fixes, arising from having `StringName` instances being destroyed after `StringName::cleanup()`.

I've been checking the code and I can see `StringName::cleanup()` is called during engine termination, which sets `configured` to `false`. `StringName`'s destructor invoked later than that just early exits because of a `!configured` check. Therefore, you shouldn't even be hitting one of those `ERR_FAIL_COND(!configured)`, which may be benign but noisy.

---

Aside, regarding this changeset as a fix, as far as my understanding of `static inline` goes, the benefits boil down to not needing both a declaration and a definition. It's syntax for fusing both so definitions can happen in multiple compilation units, with the guarantee that linking will eventually keep a single copy, just like what happens with `inline` functions.

So, I'm failing to see how `static inline` can have an influence over the predictabilty of the order in which static initializers run. If anything, I can understand your compiler's implementation may be generating a different order as a side effect of duplicate folding, which results in a more favorable outcome for `StringName` by luck.

Regardless, the changes in this PR would still be good as `static inline` has already been accepted in the codebase other times, and it would make sense to fully embrace it everywhere.
author: RandomShaper

body:
@RandomShaper Thank you for looking at this. Yes, the current implementation of ```cleanup()``` will make sure ```configured == false```. In our custom build the engine cleanup is different, that is why the issue is not reproduced on master, we should have been more specific in our description.

As we currently see it, the current code does not introduce any actual undefined behavior, but it makes it easy to introduce one by either:
- modifying ```StringName```'s default constructor to access any of its static variables (apart from ```configured```),
- modifying ```StringName```'s destructor so that it accesses any of its static variables before checking ```configured```.

The PR improves code robustness by fixing these potential instances of the [static initialization order fiasco](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/siof), which has been present in Godot because of the way non-local static variables were defined by ```StringName```. Specifically, ```StringName::mutex```, ```StringName::debug_stringname``` and ```StringName::_table``` are defined as non-inline, non-local static variables, while there is a data dependency of ```StringName```'s constructors and destructor on the initialization of these variables. This means that [ordered dynamic initialization](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/initialization#Dynamic_initialization) of ```StringName```s must happen in the same translation unit (and in the proper sequence) where the aforementioned variables are defined, and [partially-ordered](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/initialization#Dynamic_initialization) ```StringName```s must also be defined in the correct order in the translation units where those variables are defined; otherwise in the previously mentioned cases the construction and destruction of the ```StringName```s would lead to undefined behavior.

We ran into such an issue with ```default_interface``` in a custom Godot built, where the ```StringName::StringName()``` < ```StringName::mutex``` initialization sequencing caused the destructor to lock the already deinitialized mutex, causing a crash. (In our custom build the engine cleanup is different, that is why setting configured to false is not solving the issue.)

To solve these potential issues, we can simply make the [partially-ordered dynamic initialization rule](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/initialization#Dynamic_initialization) apply by making ```StringName```'s statics inline, therefore partially ordered: Because any definition of an (ordered or partially ordered) static ```StringName``` can only happen with a prior include of ```StringName```'s definition, and with it all the inline static definitions, this guarantees that in every translation unit the partially ordered variables are defined before all other ordered or partially ordered static definitions that depend on it, which guarantees correct sequencing.

Regarding the current use of ```inline``` in the Godot codebase: it has been used at several places already (e.g.: ```outdated_cache```, ```outdated_cache_dirty```, ```PARAM_PREFIX```, ```PARAMETERS_BASE_PATH```, ```VERSION```), and I would also advocate for the general use of it when defining non-local static variables to eliminate such SIOF issues and increase code robustness.
author: konczg

body:
Regarding the argument about how easy it is to introduce bugs by missing `configured` as a guard, well, my take is that anyone aspiring to maintain `StringName` should understand very well what they're doing and the role of each and every element involved.

Now, about the partially-ordered initialization, I can't but confess I wasn't aware of that rule. Now that I've parsed your statement as well as the references, I see why _using `inline` in these cases is even a better idea_ than I already thought.

For people following this conversation, let me state it clearly:

**We already have a bug by which `static StringName`s can use the shared `StringName` machinery before it has been set up (and/or after it has been torn down), leading to undefined behavior. If such machinery was using `inline`, the bug wouldn't exist.**

In conclusion, I don't see any downsides to this being merged and, on the contrary, I see a great deal of goodness in it. Regardless how safe and beneficial it looks, I'm not sure the issues being prevented or fixed are critical so not to defer it until 4.4 & 4.3.1.

Lastly, thank you for taking the time to explain the issue in detail!

It's completely broken when running on a thread, at least with `COINIT_APARTMENTTHREADED`:

> I did see EDSCALE (stands for editor scale?) is used on borders and such thing in the editor. Should that be applied here?

Yes, `vertical_padding` and `horizontal_padding` should be multiplied by `EDSCALE` when first assigned so that the padding becomes higher on hiDPI displays.

> And should vertical and horizontal_padding be change to a Size2?

Size2 is equivalent to Vector2. It's used to denote a Vector2 being used to indicate a size, as opposed to a direction vector or similar.

body:
The name of the device is `ELAN06FA:00 04F3:3214 Touchpad`. 

`BTN_GAMEPAD` should reliably detect gamepads, but unfortunately, I don't own a controller, so I cannot verify if this. According to the [Linux gamepad spec](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/v4.13/input/gamepad.html):
```
4.3. Detection
All gamepads that follow the protocol described here map BTN_GAMEPAD. 
This is an alias for BTN_SOUTH/BTN_A. 
It can be used to identify a gamepad as such. 
However, not all gamepads provide all features, so you need to test for all features that you need, first. 
...
```
author: davnotdev

body:
I don't have that many devices, so I'm not sure whether the OS distinguishes between gamepad and joystick. But [BTN_JOYSTICK](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/9d5906799f7d89c9e12f6d2e0fccb00713c945ab/include/uapi/linux/input-event-codes.h#L365C9-L365C21) also exists. Godot doesn't seem to distinguish between these two types of devices.

If it is convenient, you can use the `evtest` command line tool to test the key codes corresponding to the keys you press.
author: Rindbee

body:
In the linux-input mailing list archives, [this reply](https://patchwork.kernel.org/project/linux-input/patch/CACa7zykn0q9XJAUvrqnNATr4DUv3Kc7XujF3vm6sfRB5pE6YNQ@mail.gmail.com/#23482833) explains joystick limitations and ranges.

The joystick button mapping space is from [BTN_JOYSTICK~BTN_DEAD](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/9d5906799f7d89c9e12f6d2e0fccb00713c945ab/include/uapi/linux/input-event-codes.h#L365-L378) and [BTN_TRIGGER_HAPPY~KEY_MAX](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/9d5906799f7d89c9e12f6d2e0fccb00713c945ab/include/uapi/linux/input-event-codes.h#L767-L807). 

And `BTN_GAMEPAD` is not in that range. If this is to be believed, then joysticks are different from gamepads.

body:
Note that the original issue also refers to PCs without OpenGL support (i.e. ARM laptops without the compatibility pack installed). Falling back to Direct3D 12 on those would imply using a different rendering method – and therefore different visuals – unless ANGLE is used. I expect ANGLE to be quite a bit slower than a native D3D12 implementation.

Either way, this might be worth its own proposal so you can choose which rendering methods can fall back to other ones (e.g. falling back to Compatibility if Forward+/Mobile is not supported, or vice versa).

Not quite sure I understood your comment correctly.

> Note that the original issue also refers to PCs without OpenGL support (i.e. ARM laptops without the compatibility pack installed). Falling back to Direct3D 12 on those would imply using a different rendering method.

This PR doesn't do it, it will only fall back to Direct3D 12 from Vulkan. If native OpenGL is not supported Godot already falls back to ANGLE on Windows.

> Either way, this might be worth its own proposal so you can choose which rendering methods can fall back to other ones (e.g. falling back to Compatibility if Forward+/Mobile is not supported, or vice versa).

Agree, I think this PR is ok as is for 4.3 cause Godot already falls back to different rendering drivers within the same rendering method, this can be improved in future versions.

author: RandomShaper

body:
> Thing that would help

The crash sometimes happens when loading a certain number of scenes before the game starts. The game engine should not crash under any circumstances, so this fix is ​​necessary.

I can't provide a minimal example, because it would take too much time. It's already taken a lot of time to catch this bug, fix it and test it.

See the android-crash-3.txt file in the first post, it shows that another thread destroys the object while it is in use. MR https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94169 is unlikely to help, since the code for creating and deleting condition_variable remains unchanged.

Detailed description of incorrect work with condition_variable:
1. We start loading the resource.
2. Someone wants to get this resource, but it is not ready. The condition_variable is created and waiting occurs.
3. After the loading is complete, we call notify_all and immediately delete the condition_variable. But we have no right to do this, because another thread is using the object.
author: Ratio2

body:
I see. So, one thread may still be running `ConditionVariable::wait()` when another one decides to kill the cond var. And, even worse, multiple awaiters could end up trying to do the same. That's definitely a defect.

Now, your fix has a few code style issues, such as adding a seemingly multi-purposed helper class. The way `ResourceLoader` is written, which matches all the other lower level components in Godot overall is to favor explicitness. I'd suggest you to add instead an `awaiters_count` field to `LoadTask` and mend the logic as needed, in-place.

PS: I didn't need an MRP in the end. (Thank goodness! 😅)

body:
@akien-mga and @Geometror are we sure this code change is correct?  

I've built this locally against master, and I'm am noticing that this leads to this error.

```
ERROR: Attempt to disconnect a nonexistent connection from '[Wrapped:0]'. Signal: 'item_rect_changed', callable: 'CanvasItem::queue_redraw'.
   at: (core\object\object.cpp:1529)
```

In our extended `GraphEdit` implementation, we have two notification handlers, one for `NOTIFICATION_READY` and another for `NOTIFICATION_THEME_CHANGED`. In both of these cases, we have a handler that fires that adds/removes nodes from GraphEdit.

The theme changed event is what seems to create the issue where the `remove_child_notify` indicates that the `item_rect_changed` signal isn't connected yet to the `CanvasItem::queue_redraw` handler.

The handler that both READY and THEME_CHANGED call basically removes nodes like this:
```cpp
for (GraphNode* node : node_list) {
  remove_child(node);
  node->queue_free();
}
```
It's this that creates an issue during theme changed which wasn't an issue in Godot 4.3.stable.

What's even more bizarre is this only manifests if the UI has two `GraphEdit` instances open with two different graphs. If there is only one `GraphEdit` open, there's no issue.
